en: Prosperity!
The *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya* composed by the supreme Arhat Haribhadrasūri,
accompanied by the *Laghuvṛtti* (Short Commentary) composed by Maṇibhadra.
Having bowed to the Jina Vīra, the teacher of the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvāda), who possesses the true vision and is accompanied by the *Bhāṣāprakāśa* commentary refined with nectar,
the subject matter expressed in all philosophical systems is here briefly set forth. || 1 ||

May that Vīra be for my auspiciousness— he whose various collections of meanings became manifest upon this stainless surface of the *Sajjñānadarpaṇa* (Mirror of True Knowledge), his *Laghuvṛtti* commentary, which shines even today as if ignited by the ashes of the defects born of the Kali age.

May the illustrious Haribhadra Sūri rejoice for a long time— he by whom even a single Jaina word that brings about awakening was made fruitful on earth through his conduct, having attained the speech of the Great Lady (Śrutadevatā).
O Goddess of Speech, manifest yourself in such a way upon my six arms marked by the six systems of philosophy,
so that I may clearly expound the manifestation of those six systems!
Setting aside the extensive [version], out of compassion for beings who prefer concise works,
this clear commentary on the *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya* is composed.

For here, the venerable Śrī Haribhadrasūri—who caused the Jina-dharma to flourish by composing one hundred and fourteen treatises, whose fame was vast due to the rising light that manifested the glory of the illustrious Jina-śāsana, and who benefited the Jina-dharma—desiring to undertake this treatise for the sake of his disciples who wish to understand the nature of the definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the six philosophical systems (*ṣaḍdarśana*), and for the purpose of completing the scripture without obstacles and for the welfare of himself and others, first offers salutation to his chosen deity and states the subject matter as follows: "The True Philosophy" (*saddarśanam*).

The connection is that "meaning" (*artha*) is "declared," meaning it is "expressed. Here, the word *artha* should be understood as signifying that which is to be expressed (*abhidheya*), because the term has multiple meanings—as stated in the lexicon: "The word *artha* [is used] for the expressed, a thing, a purpose, and an accomplishment"—and because the sense is already conveyed even without the explicit mention of the word "by me" (*mayā*). What kind of meaning? It is "to be expressed in all philosophical systems" (*sarvadarśanavācya*). All those philosophical systems (*darśana*)—namely, the Buddhist, Naiyāyika, Jaina, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Jaiminīya, and so forth—are the various doctrines to be described; in these, it is "to be expressed," that is, to be told.

Having done what? Having bowed to the Jina. Having stated the general [salutation], he states the specific: which Jina? Vīra, the Lord Vardhamāna. The term "Vīra" is used with a specific intention: because the subject matter of the treatise consists of the destruction of opposing views and so forth—which is the conduct of a great warrior—and because the Blessed One, by virtue of his endurance of painful and adverse afflictions such as those involving suffering, possesses the character of a great warrior. Thus it has been said: "Because of the tearing asunder of the multitude of karmas, because of shining forth with the glory of austerity, and likewise because of your wonderful valor, the leader of the gods (Indra), out of joy for you, indeed gave you the explicit name 'Vīra'."

Thus, the author of this treatise offers a salutation to the Vīra Jina at the beginning of the work as something consistent with logical propriety; or rather, the salutation to the illustrious Tīrthaṅkara Vardhamāna is even more appropriate due to his immediate utility. He further qualifies him: of what nature is he? He is "one whose right vision (*saddarśana*) is excellent"—that is, one whose teaching (*darśana*), characterized by general comprehension or knowledge, or whose right conviction (*samyaktva*), is beautiful (*sat*).

Now, one might ask: since both right vision (*darśana*) and right conduct (*cāritra*) are limbs of liberation, why is only the single qualification "right vision" (*saddarśana*) manifested? It is not so, because of the primacy of vision alone. As the aphorism states: "Right vision should be understood here as more essential than right conduct.
Those devoid of conduct may attain perfection, but those devoid of vision do not attain perfection."
"One who has fallen from right conduct must grasp the vision (darśana) here more firmly;

those devoid of conduct may succeed, but those devoid of vision do not succeed. Thus, that very qualification is appropriate. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "the indicator of the doctrine of manifoldness" (syādvādadeśaka). Syādvāda is a discourse characterized by manifold possibilities (syāt); it consists of being and non-being, permanence and impermanence, expressibility and inexpressibility, and the nature of generality and particularity. That which points out—that is, teaches this—to the faithful is [the doctrine].

In the first half-verse here, the Lord’s fourfold excellence (*atiśaya*) is implied: by the term “one with true vision” (*saddarśana*), because vision and knowledge always accompany one another, there is the excellence of knowledge; by the terms “the Victor” (*jina*) and “the Hero” (*vīra*), because he is the conqueror of passion and the like, and the dispeller of the eight karmas and other misfortunes, there is the excellence of the removal of misfortune (*apāyāpagama*); by the term “teacher of the doctrine of manifoldness” (*syādvādadeśaka*), there is the excellence of speech (*vacana*); and since being served by hosts of gods and demons filled with incessant devotion is a natural consequence for one of such a nature, there is the excellence of worship (*pūjā*). || 1 ||
In this regard, with respect to the fundamental divisions, there are exactly six systems of philosophy;
these should be understood by the wise according to the distinctions among their deities and principles. || 2 ||

What are those philosophical systems (*darśanas*)? He states their number individually: "the philosophical systems. In this world, there are only six well-known philosophical systems; the word "only" (*eva*) is used for emphasis, even though many philosophical systems are well known through their various divisions and subdivisions. As it is said in the Sūtra:
"There are one hundred and eight [schools] of the Kriyāvādins, and eighty-four of the Akriyāvādins."
The Annāṇiya have seventy-seven, and the Veṇaiya have thirty-two.
"There are one hundred and eighty proponents of non-action (*akriyāvādin*), eighty-four proponents of the self (*ātmavādin*), and thirty-two proponents of discipline (*vinayavādin*). Thus,

there are three hundred and sixty-three heretical sects (*pāṣaṇḍika*), along with the eighteen divisions of the Buddhist schools— such as the Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, Mādhyamika, and others— and the many divisions among the disciples of Jaimini.
Utpala knows the kārikās; Prabhākara knows the tantra; Vāmana knows both; but Revana knows nothing at all.
There are also many internal subdivisions, such as the Bahūdakas, Kuṭīcaras, Haṃsas, Paramahaṃsas, Bhaṭṭas, Prābhākaras, and others.

Furthermore, because of differences in their fundamental principles (tattva), deities, means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and so forth, many subdivisions appear within other philosophical systems as well; nevertheless, since they are ultimately included within these [six], the term "six" is used with this restrictive qualification.

Now, one might ask: "Since there are indefinite combinations [of views], why are there only six? To this he says: "With reference to the fundamental divisions. This means that there are exactly six fundamental divisions; with reference to them—that is, relying upon them—the wise, the learned, should know and understand these philosophical systems (*darśanas*).

In what manner? By means of the distinction between the deities (*devatā*) and the principles (*tattva*). The deities are those who preside over the visions, while the principles are the secrets that bring about liberation. The meaning is that by their distinction, the various deities of the visions and the principles of the visions are to be known individually. || 2 ||
Bauddha, Naiyāyika, Sāṃkhya, Jaina, Vaiśeṣika, and likewise Jaiminīya—oh, these are the names of the philosophical systems (darśanas). (3)
He states the names of those very systems of philosophy (darśana) with the words "Bauddham" (the Buddhist).

The word "aho" is used for addressing or drawing attention; the summary is that these are the names of the philosophical systems (mata), and the verb "should be known" (jñeyāni)—though unstated, like the verbs "asti" or "bhavati"—is to be understood.

In this context, "Bauddha" refers to the Saugata system, so called because Buddha is its deity (*bauddham iti buddho devatāsyeti bauddham*). "Naiyāyika" refers to the Pāśupata system; its etymological derivation is that it is "Naiyāyika" because it does not depart from *nyāya*, which is the path of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-mārga*). "Sāṃkhya" refers to the Kāpila system; this is a name based on the Primordial Puruṣa (*ādi-puruṣa*). "Jaina" refers to the Ārhata system, so called because Jina is its deity (*jainam iti jino devatāsyeti jainam*). "Vaiśeṣika" refers to the system of Kaṇāda. Although there is equality among these systems regarding their philosophical views, deities, and so forth, [the Vaiśeṣika is distinguished] from the Naiyāyikas by its collection of categories such as substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*).

"Viśiṣṭa" means Vaiśeṣika; "Jaiminīya" refers to the system of the sage Jaimini, namely the Bhāṭṭa-darśana. The word "ca" (and) indicates a conjunction. Thus, it should be understood that these are the names of the six systems of philosophy (ṣaddarśana) that must be known by the disciple. || 3 ||
[The Buddhist Doctrine] Regarding that, in the Buddhist doctrine, the deity is said to be the Sugata, the one who has thoroughly explained the four noble truths beginning with suffering. (4)
Now, because it was presented first in the introductory verse, he explains the Buddhist doctrine at the outset with the word "therein" (tatra).

In that regard, within that Buddhist system, the teaching of the Sugata, first of all—“Sugata” being the deity, the Buddha as the deity, the venerable Buddha who performs the acts of showing and so forth—"kila" indicates a traditional report from authoritative sources. He qualifies him further: of what nature is he? One who explains, shows, or tells by way of determining reality (*tattva*). Of what things? He says: of the Noble Truths (*āryasatya*), that is, of the realities designated as the Noble Truths. How many in number? Four, consisting of four forms.

Of what nature are they? He says: "of suffering and so forth," meaning those characterized by suffering, its origin, the path, and cessation; here, the word *ādi* (and so forth) has the sense of a constituent part (*avayava*). As it is said: "The wise man should recognize the word *ādi* as having four meanings: capacity, arrangement, manner, and likewise a constituent part."
Thus, the meaning is that such a Sugata is to be known as the deity in the Buddhist system. || 4 ||
The aggregates of one in saṃsāra are suffering, and they are proclaimed to be fivefold:
consciousness, sensation, perception, mental formations, and form.

Explaining the very first reality, he says: "Suffering. To the question, "What is called suffering?"—in response to this doubt—he says: "The aggregates of the transmigrator. The term *saṃsārin* means those that transmigrate; the aggregates (*skandhas*) are things characterized by expansion, specific accumulations. The meaning is that in *saṃsāra*, these exist in the form of accumulation and depletion. And those aggregates are proclaimed to be five; they are stated to be five in number. Which are they? He says:
"Consciousness, sensation, perception, mental formations, and form itself. Thus.
In this context, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to specific cognition regarding the momentariness of all things. As it has been said:
"Whatever exists is momentary, like a rain-cloud; and these entities exist.
Here, the power of existence (*sattā-śakti*) is established by valid cognition (*miti*) in respect to effective action (*arthakriyā*); and that [power] is established in those things already proven."
"Nor can there be only one kind [of action], nor could it be that another's action is never performed;
for in both ways, the occurrence of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is consistent, and thus it rests upon the probandum.

Thus: "Cognition (vijñāna), sensation (vedanā)," etc. Sensation is so called because it is sensed; it consists of the experience of pleasure and pain, bound by the transformation of merit and demerit from previous existences. A monk, while wandering for alms, said this when a thorn became stuck in his foot:
"Monks, ninety-one eons ago, a man was killed by me with a spear; through the ripening of that karma, my foot is now pierced."

And so forth. "Designation" (*saṃjñā*) refers to the object named "designation"; all this worldly activity consisting of the nature of sentient and insentient beings is merely designation, merely a name. Herein, neither the relationship with wife, son, friend, brother, and so on, nor the multitude of objects such as pots and cloths, is ultimately real. And thus says that Sūtra:

"O monks, these are merely designations, merely conventional usage, merely conceptual constructions, and merely worldly conventions: the past time, the future time, destruction with its cause, space, the person (*pudgala*), and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). In this context, 'conditioned phenomenon' refers to the arising of a cognition in the form of 'this is that very Devadatta' or 'this is that very lamp-flame,' occurring in a cognizer who possesses a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) corresponding to a prior state, awakened by the observation of the continuity of objects belonging to another existence. As it has been said:
'For within that very continuum in which the latencies of karma have been deposited...'"

"It bears fruit in that very [substratum], just as redness [is produced] in cotton. Regarding "form" (*rūpa*): it is an accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu*) shimmering with various colors. For in the Buddhist system, since the gross form of the multitude of objects appearing in the world is refuted by the logical arguments of those who see [reality], only atoms are ultimately real. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "but," while "eva" (only/just) serves as a filler for the verse. || 5 ||
That from which the entire host of passion and the like arises in the world—consisting of what is called the nature of "self" and "mine"—is recognized as the origin (*samudaya*). (6)
Having analyzed the Noble Truth named suffering through its fivefold division, he states its nature as the reality of the collection of objects, beginning with the words "it arises."

Because, from which [cause] the entire, complete host of passion and the rest—that is, attachment, aversion, and delusion—arises and originates in the world; of what nature is it? To this he says: it is called the nature of "self" and "mine. This notion that "this is the self" and "this is mine," or through the metaphorical application of a collection of words, that "this is another" and "this belongs to another," is the basis for attachment and aversion. The host of passion and the rest, rooted in that and designated by it, arises in the form of attachment through the aspect of "self" and "mine," and in the form of aversion through the transformation of "belonging to another. That from which it arises is the *samudaya* (the origin).
The reality known as "name" (nāma-tattva) is accepted and intended in the Buddhist philosophy. || 6 ||
That habitual tendency (vāsanā) which is [the realization] that "all conditioned phenomena are momentary" should be known as the Path; cessation is called liberation.
Now, elaborating upon the third and fourth principles, he says: "All conditioned phenomena are momentary" (*kṣaṇikāḥ*).

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskārāḥ*) are momentary; that is, those streams of cognition (*jñānasantāna*) which arise—characterized by such mental impressions as "this is that very same thing"—regarding all things such as pots, cloths, pillars, and lotuses existing within the recesses of the three worlds during their second and subsequent moments, are momentary when they come under the scope of investigation. This is what they establish through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The entire argument—that "everything that exists is momentary, because in what is non-momentary there is a contradiction regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) due to the impossibility of either successive or simultaneous action"—should also be inferred to apply to the locus of the debate, as it establishes no distinction regarding momentariness. Furthermore, the proof of this distinction is as follows: when the totality of conditions such as a mallet is present, the entire collection of produced entities, such as pots and cloths, is perceived to be perishable. In that regard, does this nature of destruction, which exists in its final state, exist at the time of the entity’s production or not? If it does exist, then [momentariness] follows.

It must perish immediately after the moment of its arising; or else, if its very nature is such that it must perish only after remaining for some time, then even when a mallet or other instrument is brought near, this same nature would persist, and it would have to remain for that same duration once again. Thus, even if a hundred blows from a mallet were to fall, no destruction would occur, and the jar would endure for aeons. Consequently, one who does not wish to incur the sin of destroying the established order of worldly affairs must necessarily accept the momentary flux (*kṣaṇakṣayitva*) of all things.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: An entity is of a perishable nature even at the time of its origination, because it has the essential nature of perishing; whatever is perishable is of that very nature even at the time of its origination, just like the nature of a jar existing in its final moment; and form, taste, and so forth, possess the essential nature of perishing from the very moment they arise—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Now, if all things are momentary, how is it that there arises the cognition based on mental impressions (*vāsanā*) that "this is that very same thing"? It is said in reply: because of the arising of consciousness through the perception of a continuous succession of similar moments, and due to the connection with *vidyā* (innate knowledge), at the very moment of the dissolution of the preceding moment, an impression is produced—just as in the case of a lamp-flame, where one thinks "this is that same lamp-flame"—and a subsequent moment similar to it arises. Thus, through the long-term transformation resulting from familiarity with a series of cognitions of identical form, and because of their uninterrupted emergence, [the illusion of identity occurs].

Even when preceding moments are utterly destroyed, the determination that "this is that very same thing" forcibly arises; and indeed, such a recognition as "this is that very same thing" is observed in the case of nails, hair, and the like, which have been cut off and grown back again. Why, then, should a wise person not consider this possible here as well? Therefore, the proof that "whatever exists is momentary" is established, and the impression (*vāsanā*) that "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary" is logically consistent.

He states the subject at hand: "In this way, whatever latent impression (*vāsanā*) exists, that is to be known and understood here in the Buddhist system as the Noble Truth called the Path (*mārga*). The word *tu* serves to include the subsequent meaning while also acting as a conjunction for the preceding. He states the fourth Noble Truth: in response to the doubt "What is cessation (*nirodha*)?", liberation (*mokṣa*) is declared; liberation is *apavarga*. The meaning is that cessation, which consists of the latent impressions of universal momentariness and universal selflessness, is designated as the Noble Truth [of Cessation]. || 7 ||
The five sense-faculties, the five objects such as sound, the mind, and the sphere of phenomena—these are the twelve spheres (āyatana). || 8 ||
Having thus explained the principles (*tattva*), he now describes the bases (*āyatana*) which are connected to them, beginning with "the five sense organs" (*pañcendriyāṇi*).

The five in number are the sense organs consisting of touch, taste, smell, sight, and hearing; the five objects, such as sound, are sound, form, taste, touch, and smell—the meaning is that these five objects are the functions of the sense organs. "The mental" (*mānasa*) is the mind (*citta*); "the base of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana*) means a base where phenomena are predominant, which is to say, the locus of consciousness.

These twelve should be known; not only are these the twelve bases (āyatana), but birth, old age and death, existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, name-and-form, consciousness, mental formations, and ignorance are also the twelve bases. The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction; all these formations (saṃskāra) are momentary, and the rest is exactly as before. || 8 ||
In the Buddhist philosophy, two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are to be known:
perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna), because correct knowledge (samyagjñāna) is of two kinds. (9)

Having explained the principles (*tattva*), he now states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—beginning with the word "pramāṇa. The word "tathā" (thus) serves to connect the present topic; in the Buddhist system, that is, in the Buddhist doctrine, two means of valid cognition are to be known. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "furthermore. He states those very two: perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). "Perception" means that which has gone toward each sense-organ (*akṣa*); that is, it is sensory. "Inference" means that by which something is inferred; that is, it is inferential.

Since right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is a certain comprehension that is twofold—meaning it is of two kinds—the inclusion of the term "right" (*samyak*) is for the purpose of excluding false knowledge; the meaning is that it consists solely of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). || 9 ||
Let it be understood that perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous;
whereas the knowledge of the probandum (liṅgin) derived from a three-featured logical mark (liṅga) is designated as inference. 10.

Anticipating the doubt—namely, "What kind of perception (pratyakṣa) is to be understood here, given the fear of confusion regarding the definitions that depend on distinct perspectives?"—he says: "Perception" (pratyakṣam).

In this context, let perception be understood—that is, known—by the student through both means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Of what nature is it? It is "free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha). A conceptual construction is a cognition associated with words; that which is free from or devoid of such is non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka); this is the meaning.

Furthermore, that which is non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), free from delusion, and characterized by atoms (*paramāṇu*) appearing as such—namely, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—is indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and non-erroneous. On the other hand, cognition associated with external, gross objects such as pots and cloths is conceptual (*savikalpaka*). Since those external, gross objects will be refuted through the arguments and logical proofs of their respective systems, it is only the nature of the atoms in the form of blue and so forth that possesses ultimate reality.

If it is asked: "But if external objects do not exist, then what is the object of this gross external appearance of jars, cloths, carts, and so forth? [The answer is: This is indeed without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), set in motion by beginningless, false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); it is a mere semblance of worldly transaction (*vyavahārābhāsa*) because it is devoid of an object, like the vision of hairs in the sky or like dream-cognition. As it has been said: "There is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there any other experience of it;
due to the absence of the grasped and the grasper, that very [intellect] shines by itself."
"For no external object exists in the way it is conceptualized by the ignorant;
rather, the mind, stirred up by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), proceeds toward the appearance of objects. Thus [it is said].

Thus it has been said: "Perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous. He states the definition of inference: furthermore, that knowledge of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin)—such as fire—derived from the mark (liṅga)—such as smoke—which possesses the three characteristics consisting of presence in the subject (pakṣadharmatva), presence in similar instances (sapakṣasattva), and absence from dissimilar instances (vipakṣavyāvṛtti), is designated as inference; the meaning is that it is the means of valid cognition known as inference. Since the definition is already established in the aphorism, there is no fault even if the final word consists of nine syllables rather than eight. || 10 ||

Visible forms [are the subject]; let the three characteristics of the reason—its presence in the subject, its existence in the similar class, and its absence from the dissimilar class—be thus discerned. (11)

He states the three forms themselves: "the forms" (rūpāṇi). The connection is that the three forms of the reason (*hetu*), which is the means of inference (*anumāna*), should be discerned. Among these, "presence in the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) means that the subject (*pakṣa*) is the locus qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); for example, in the case "this mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," the mountain is the subject. Therein, the property is "possessing smoke," which is pervaded by "possessing fire"—meaning that smoke does not deviate from fire. "Presence in the similar instance" (*sapakṣe sattva*) means: whatever possesses smoke, that possesses fire, just as the kitchen area.

In this context, the meaning is that by means of the reason (*hetu*) "possessing smoke" (*dhūmavattva*), there is presence (*sattva*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), namely the kitchen, in the form of "possessing fire" (*vahnimattva*). Regarding the absence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), it means that where fire is absent, smoke is also absent, as in a body of water. For in a body of water, the property of possessing fire, upon being excluded, excludes the pervaded property of possessing smoke along with it. In this manner, the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) of the reason should be understood. || 11 ||
This summary of what is to be stated according to the Buddhist tenets has been presented;
now let the system of the Naiyāyikas, which is being told, be heard. (12)

Introducing [the next section], he says: "The Buddhist doctrine... This summary has been presented, explained, and brought to its conclusion. Of what? Of that which is to be expressed (*vācya*) in the Buddhist doctrine (*bauddharāddhānta*); that is, the meaning (*artha*) to be denoted within the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of the Buddhists. Immediately following this, the summary of the Naiyāyika system, the teaching of Śiva (*śivaśāsana*), is being told: "Listen as it is being told"—that is, let it be heard as it is being narrated. (12)
[The Naiyāyika view:
In the system of Akṣapāda, the god Śiva is the agent of creation and dissolution;
he is omnipresent, eternal, one, omniscient, and the substratum of eternal consciousness. (13)

He says that very thing: "Ākṣapāda," etc. The Ākṣapādas are the Naiyāyikas; in their system or teaching, the God who presides over the vision [of truth] is Śiva Maheśvara. Of what nature is he? He is the "performer of creation and destruction" (*sṛṣṭisaṃhārakṛt*). Creation is the birth of living beings, and destruction is their dissolution; "creation and destruction" is a *dvandva* compound, and he who performs these two is formed with the suffix *kvip*, with *t* as the final letter. For instance, it must be understood that there exists some Person of indescribable majesty who is the creator of this world, whose nature as consisting of the moving and the unmoving is perceived through direct observation. And regarding mere creation alone...

Since there is no one who can act as a mother for the infinite multitude of living beings arising incessantly even within the three worlds, some agent of destruction must necessarily be admitted. The proof for this is as follows: everything—such as the earth, mountains, trees, cities, and walls—is preceded by an intelligent agent, because it is an effect. Whatever is an effect is preceded by an intelligent agent, just like a pot. This [world] is an effect; therefore, it is preceded by an intelligent agent. The meaning is that this [agent] is indeed the Lord (Īśvara).

If there were a difference [between the world and its cause], then the sky would be [the counter-example]; yet this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is universally known in the world that the earth, mountains, and so forth are effects, either by virtue of being produced from a collection of their own causes or by virtue of being composite wholes (*avayavin*). Nor do the faults of being contradictory (*viruddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) apply, because the reason is absolutely excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). It is not "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because the subject (*dharmin*) possesses properties that are not sublated by perception, inference, comparison, or scripture. Nor is it "neutralized by an equal counter-argument" (*prakaraṇasama*), because there is no emergence of a counter-inference based on the established nature of a category that opposes it.

If it is argued that there is no absence of the fallacy of *prakaraṇasama* because a counter-inference arises—namely, that God cannot be the agent of creation and dissolution precisely because He is, like one whose self is extinguished (*nirvṛtātman*), devoid of a body (*aśarīratva*)—how can this be so?

It is replied: In this context, does your well-wisher accept the subject (*dharmin*)—the Lord (*īśvara*) who is being established—as something perceived or unperceived? If it is unperceived, then there follows the fallacy of the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for the reason (*hetu*) imagined by you. If, however, it is perceived, then why is that very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which it is perceived not also accepted as manifesting its own body? Therefore, how can it be bodiless? Thus, the reason is not defective; it has been rightly stated that Śiva is the creator of creation and dissolution, and likewise all-pervading (*vibhu*).

He is all-pervasive; for if he were restricted to residing in a single location, it would be impossible for him to fashion objects situated in various indefinite places according to their specific and exact forms. Indeed, even a potter stationed in one place does not exert himself toward the production of jars located far and far away. Therefore, the Blessed One is omnipresent (*vibhu*). Likewise, he is eternal and one—meaning he is both eternal and one. Because he is eternal, he is therefore one; for that which is eternal is of a stable, unitary nature, neither falling away nor arising. For if the Blessed One were non-eternal...
Because it depends on another for its arising, it follows that it is produced; for an entity is considered "produced" (kṛtaka) when its own origination requires the operation of something else.

Now, if someone were to assert another creator of the world, he too must be questioned: is he eternal or non-eternal? If he is eternal, what fault has been committed against the Lord under discussion? If he is non-eternal, then because of that very non-eternality, there must be another producer for him as well, and for him yet another; thus, by accepting hundreds of such artisan-like conceptual constructions regarding the alternatives of eternal and non-eternal, there would be no end to the debate even at the end of a kalpa. Therefore, the Blessed One is indeed eternal. Furthermore, He is one and without a second; for if the status of being the creator of the world were accepted for many, [chaos would ensue].

If each individual entity were to create its own dissimilar form through excessive independent activity, everything would fall into total disorder; therefore, it is logically consistent that the Blessed One is one alone. Thus, the qualification "eternally one" is appropriate. Likewise, he is "omniscient," meaning the knower of all particulars regarding all entities. For, in the absence of omniscience, he would lack the capacity to correctly assemble the collection of scattered atomic particles spread throughout the world, which are necessary for the production of the intended objects.

The construction and arrangement of objects according to their true nature is difficult to accomplish; yet, who would not approve of one who, being omniscient, fashions the things to be produced in accordance with the spherical dimensions corresponding to the combined and appropriate collection of causes for all living beings, and grants the experience of pleasure and pain in heaven and hell according to the measure of the merit and demerit earned by each? As it has been said:
"Impelled by God, a being may go either to heaven or to the pit;
this ignorant creature is not its own master over its own happiness and sorrow."

Further qualifying [the Lord], he says: "the locus of eternal consciousness" (*nityabuddhisamāśraya*). For one who possesses momentary consciousness lacks true agency because of dependence on external factors for the accomplishment of effects; thus, the consequence would be a lack of sovereignty (*anīśvaratva*). Śiva, characterized by such qualities, must be accepted according to the Nyāya school. || 13 ||
In this system, there are sixteen principles, beginning with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth; namely:
the means of valid cognition, the object of valid cognition, doubt, and purpose. (14)
The example (dṛṣṭānta), the tenet (siddhānta), the members of the syllogism (avayava), reasoning (tarka), and the conclusion (nirṇaya);
debate (vāda), contentious discussion (jalpa), destructive criticism (vitaṇḍā), fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), and quibbles (chala). || 15 ||
The classification of the types of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is thus described.
Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is the cause for the apprehension of an object, is of four kinds. (16)

Now, explaining the categories (*tattvas*), he says with the words beginning "the categories" and so forth. In this context, within the system under discussion—the Nyāya school—there are sixteen categories, starting with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To facilitate understanding for beginners, he states their names as follows: "The attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of the truth regarding the means of valid cognition, the objects of valid cognition, doubt, purpose, example, tenet, members of a syllogism, reasoning, ascertainment, debate, sophistry, cavil, fallacies of the reason, quibble, futile rejoinder, and points of defeat. Thus, there are sixteen; such is the exposition of these categories, that is, the exposition of the categories in this manner.

The meaning is the manifestation of [the categories] by name alone. Now, he states the individual nature of each; therein, first, revealing the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "The cause of the apprehension of an object is the means of valid cognition. The apprehension of an object—that is, a thing—is knowledge; its cause or instrument is the means of valid cognition. Because the number of means of valid cognition is not fixed according to the perspectives of higher and lower systems, he speaks to instruct one who is doubting regarding their number: "That is fourfold. That means of valid cognition is to be known as being of four kinds. (14–16)
Perception, inference, comparison, and likewise verbal testimony—[perception] is that which arises from the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects and is non-erroneous. (17)
Knowledge that consists of ascertainment and is free from verbal designation is perception; other means of knowledge are preceded by that [perception] and are of three kinds. (18)

In this context, regarding the fourfold classification of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the connection [of the question] is: "What is perception (*pratyakṣa*) like? He states the qualifiers: "arisen from the contact of the sense-organ with its object" (*indriyārthasannikarṣotpannam*). "Sense-organ" (*indriya*) and "object" (*artha*) form a copulative compound (*dvandva*); [perception is] that which has arisen or been produced from their contact, that is, from conjunction (*saṃyoga*). For the sense-organ, due to proximity, comes into contact with the object; from the conjunction of the sense-organ and the object, knowledge is produced. As it has been said: "The self unites with the mind, the mind with the sense-organ, and the sense-organ with its own object—this is the rapid sequence."
This alone is yoga of the mind; what indeed is inaccessible to it?
Wherever the mind goes, there this Self has gone.

In this context, "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārika*) means that which does not turn out otherwise when verified by another cognition. For instance, the cognition of silver in a fragment of mother-of-pearl is seen to be erroneous even though it arises from the contact of the sense organ with the object; therefore, "non-erroneous" must be included as a qualification. Likewise, "of the nature of determination" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) means that which establishes practical activity (*vyavahāra*). For example, the cognition of water arising from the proximity of the sense organ to an object—even amidst a dense thicket of grass and trees on a watery ground—is invalid because it fails to establish practical activities such as bathing or drinking upon reaching that place.
Therefore, the qualification "of the nature of determination" is added to mean that which is fruitful.

"Likewise, it is devoid of designation (*vyapadeśa*). Designation means error; it is free from that. For instance, in a person whose eyes are afflicted by defects such as cataracts or jaundice from birth, a cognition of yellow arises regarding a white conch shell. Although that cognition exists at all times—produced by the contact of the sense-organ with its object due to the non-cessation of those ocular defects—it is not perception according to the aforementioned definition, because it is the cognition of one thing as something else. Thus, the four qualifiers have been stated to establish the nature of perception.

Now he states inference (*anumāna*): "He teaches that inference is another means of knowledge (*māna*"; that inference would first—meaning initially—be threefold, consisting of three types. By the word "first" (*pūrva*), he indicates the infinity of the internal subdivisions of inference—namely, that it is "first" [in the sense of being preceded by] perception (*pratyakṣa-pūrva*). This is the meaning of the two verses. || 17–18 ||
It is observed as being like the "prior" (pūrvavat), like the "residual" (śeṣavat), and likewise as "general" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa);
among these, the first is here proclaimed as inference from cause to effect.
He states the threefold nature of inference: "pūrvavat" (as before), etc.

The three types of inference are *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*. The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction; "eva" (only/just) is for the sake of completion; and "tathā" (thus) is for illustration. Among those three, the first type of inference is mentioned here—in this treatise—wherein an effect is inferred from a cause. Since the effect characterized by rain is known from the cause, namely the cloud, that is called the inference named "cause-to-effect. This is the meaning. || 19 ||
As before, the garden is described:
"In this world, clouds of such a nature—possessing a dark luster like that of bees, buffalo-horns, serpents, and *tāla* trees—never fail to bring rain. (20)
Strengthening that very point by means of an illustration, he says: "rolambā... and so forth.

The word *yathā* marks the beginning of the statement of an example. *Rolambāḥ* are bees; *gavalam* is the horn of a buffalo; *vyālāḥ* are elephants or serpents; *tamālāḥ* are specific types of trees—all these objects are to be understood as being black by their very nature. The compounds are both *dvandva* and *bahuvrīhi*. Clouds (*payomucaḥ*) of this kind do not fail to produce rain. By the phrase "of this kind" (*evam-prāyāḥ*), other causes of rain, such as specific signs like rising vapors, are also to be understood. As it has been said:
The deep-thundering onset of these clouds has split the mountain caves,
and their lofty forms have become tawny from contact with the high-reaching streaks of lightning.
These and others likewise do not deviate from rain. || 20 ||

Inference from the remainder (*śeṣavat-anumāna*)—that which is an inference of a cause from an effect—is considered "possessing a remainder" (*śeṣavat*). For example, from such a flood in a river, one infers that it has rained upstream. (21)
He states the second variety of inference, called *śeṣavat*, with the words "from the effect" (*kāryāt*).

That inference from an effect—that is, from a result—to an cause, which is the comprehension of the entity that served as the cause for the production of the result, is considered and taught in the Nyāya system as *śeṣavat* inference. For example, from a river-flood characterized by a mass of flowing water, one infers that a cloud has rained above; that knowledge of the downpour from the cloud upon the mountain peak, derived from such a swelling of the river's current, is *śeṣavat*.
In this case, the effect is the swelling of the river, and the cause is that rain has fallen upon the mountain. And it has been said by the Naiyāyikas:
"The water is vast and turbid, characterized by the whirling of eddies;
it is marked by masses of foam bursting forth from the violent impact of the waves."
"Even this extraordinary flood of the river, crowded with abundant *śaivāla* moss, fruit, and grassy meadows, cannot be fully described. (21)
Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*):

That which is [inferred] through general observation is as follows: the arrival of a person at another location is preceded by motion; since that is so for a person, it is likewise so for the sun. (22)

He states the third type of inference with the words "And that which... (*yacca*). The particle *ca* has the sense of "furthermore. That inference which is "based on general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is of this kind: for example, in the case of a person (*pums*), such as Devadatta, arrival at another place is preceded by motion; that is to say, moving from one location to another location is preceded by the act of going. Just as Devadatta, having set out from Ujjayinī, reached the city of Māhiṣmatī, so it is with the sun as well; just as it is with the person, so too is that motion accepted in the case of the sun.

Although the motion of the sun moving through the sky is not perceived due to the absence of its appearance before the eyes, nevertheless, its descent from the mountain of sunrise to the peak of the mountain of sunset indicates that motion.
In this way, it should be understood that this is an inference based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa). || 22 ||
Comparison is declared to be the means of establishing that which is not yet known by means of its similarity to a well-known thing, as for example: "As is a cow, so is a gavaya."

Now, although verbal testimony (śabda-pramāṇa) follows in sequence, it is set aside due to its limited scope; therefore, he first states the definition of comparison (upamāna): "prasiddhi... [and so forth].

That which is being stated is called "analogy" (*upamāna*), as it has been explained; for there is an inseparable connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*. What is it? It is the establishment of what is not yet established—that is, the making known of an object that is currently unknown. This is done "by means of similarity to a property well-known [to both parties]. That property (*dharma*) which is recognized by everyone from children to cowherds and women—its similarity (*sādharmya*), meaning its state of possessing common characteristics—is the basis for what is called analogy. He provides an example: "As is a cow, so is a gavaya."

For example, suppose a forest-dweller is asked by a city-dweller, "What is a *gavaya* like? Being familiar with the characteristics of both the cow (*go*) and the *gavaya*, he says to the city-dweller: "As is the cow, so is the *gavaya*; it possesses hooves, a hump, a tail, a dewlap, and so forth. The meaning is that just as the cow is [well-known], the *gavaya*—which is established by birth—is to be understood in the same way. Here, the well-known cow serves as the means of establishing the unknown *gavaya* through its similarity (*sādharmya*). || 23 ||
Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person; thus, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is fourfold.
The objects of cognition (prameya), however, consist of the self, the body, the objects [of the senses], the intellect, the sense organs, and so forth. (24)

Having described comparison (*upamāna*), he states the means of valid cognition consisting of verbal testimony (*śabda*): "Verbal testimony" (*śābda*). Furthermore, verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*). A reliable person is one who speaks truthfully and is well-wishing; the instruction of such a trustworthy person—that is, his declarative statement—is to be known as verbal testimony, the means of valid cognition called scripture (*āgama*). Thus, by the manner explained, the means of knowledge (*māna*)—that is, the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is established as fourfold, meaning it consists of four types.

Now he states the definition of the object of cognition (*prameya*): "The object of cognition, moreover, consists of the self, the body, the objects, the intellect, the senses, pleasure, and so forth. An object of cognition is an entity that is graspable by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The word "moreover" (*tu*) serves as a particle of emphasis. "Self and body" is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of the remaining six categories of objects of cognition.

And that [object of knowledge] is twelvefold according to the Nyāya-sūtra, categorized as: self (ātman), body (śarīra), sense organs (indriya), objects (artha), intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), activity (pravṛtti), defects (doṣa), rebirth (pretyabhāva), fruit (phala), suffering (duḥkha), and liberation (apavarga). Among these, the self is established through attributes such as sentience, agency, and omnipresence; likewise, the body and the others are to be understood as objects of knowledge. However, they have not been elaborated upon here for fear of excessive length in the text, and because they are easily understood from other treatises. || 24 ||

A cognition that is characterized by doubt as to "what is this? is considered *saṃśaya* (doubt). That which one proceeds to see [in order to resolve it] is the *prayojana* (purpose), which is to be accomplished. || 25 ||

He states the nature of doubt and the other [categories] with the words beginning "What is this? When one perceives an object from a distance, being uncertain regarding the characteristics that determine its identity, one says: "What is this?"—namely, "Is this a post or a person? That cognition which is characterized by such uncertainty is considered and accepted as the specific category known as *saṃśaya* (doubt) in that system of instruction.

He states the purpose (*prayojana*): "But as for that which is called the 'purpose,' what is its nature? He says: "Because of desire (*arthitva*), a living being engages in an action toward an object to be accomplished; [the word] 'having perceived' (*pratītya*) is to be supplied [to the verse]. For there is no undertaking of an action that is fruitless; thus, it is said 'because of desire. The meaning is that such engagement is the purpose. (25)
The example, however, must be something that is not a subject of dispute; the tenet, moreover, is of four kinds, based on the distinction between "common to all systems" and so forth. (26)

Furthermore, this so-called "example" (dṛṣṭānta) must be a reality; what is it? It is not an object of dispute—that is to say, when a statement is presented, it does not become a subject of debate, meaning that no dispute arises as to whether "this is thus" or "is it not. Moreover, the meaning is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) only so long as it does not stumble due to the lack of clear support from an example. And it has been said: "The meaning of an argument moves about as soon as it enters the range of the mind, until it is firmly supported by an example."

This is the illustration to be understood. Furthermore, the established tenet (*siddhānta*) is of four kinds; as to how this is so, he says: "by way of the divisions beginning with *sarvatantra*. The first division is the *sarvatantra-siddhānta*. From the word "beginning" (*ādi*), these three other divisions are to be known: namely, the *pratitantra-siddhānta*, the *adhikaraṇa-siddhānta*, and the *abhyupagama-siddhānta*. These are the four divisions of the established tenet. This is merely a statement of their names; however, the specific details should be learned from extensive treatises. || 26 ||
The thesis, the reason, the example, the application, and likewise the conclusion—these are the five members; reasoning (tarka) is that which brings an end to doubt.
Just as one infers that there must be a post here from the landing of crows and the like, so too is a conviction following doubt and reasoning considered a definitive conclusion (nirṇaya). || 28 ||
He states the nature of the three principles beginning with the members [of a syllogism] by means of the passage beginning with "pratijñā" (the proposition).

The connection is that there are five members. He states the first half [of the verse]: the five members are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). Among these, the proposition is the subject (*pakṣa*) qualified by the property to be proved (*sādhya*), such as "this mountain possesses fire. The reason is the statement of the mark (*liṅga*), such as "because of possessing smoke. The example is the statement of the illustration (*udāharaṇa*), such as "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, just like the kitchen area. The application is the statement that summarizes the reason.

"This possesses smoke," and so forth; the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) by means of the instruction of the reason (*hetvapadeśa*), such as "therefore, it possesses fire," and so forth. Thus, the nature of the five members (*pañcāvayava*) has been defined; this should be understood as the reality of the members (*avayavatattva*). Hypothetical reasoning (*tarka*) is the cessation of doubt (*saṃśayoparama*). For example, "like the crow," and so forth. When an object is within the range of vision from a distance, because there is no clear manifestation, one wonders: "Is this a post or a person? When that doubt ceases—that is, when it is absent—hypothetical reasoning occurs; this is what is meant by the reality called *tarka*. To explain how this is so, he says: "For example."

Having observed an object situated at a distance and being in doubt as to whether it is a post or a person, one becomes attentive and reflects: from the arrival of crows and so forth—the word "and so forth" including the creeping of vines and other characteristics of a post—it must be a post; because of its connection with crows and the like, there must be a post here, for in the case of a person, the arrival of crows would be impossible due to head-shaking, hand-waving, and other such movements. Thus, when doubt has ceased, the nature of *tarka* (reasoning) is to be understood.

"Beyond," and so forth: that cognition which arises subsequent to the previously mentioned doubt (*saṃdeha*) and deliberation (*tarka*), having as its objective the realization "this is indeed a post" or "this is indeed a person," is *nirṇaya* (ascertainment). It should be understood as a specific category of reality named ascertainment; and because of the connection with the meaning [of the preceding terms], those two [doubt and deliberation] are to be understood even though they were not explicitly mentioned here. (27–28)
That which arises from the teacher and the disciple adopting opposing positions for the purpose of practicing debate is called *vāda* (discussion). || 29 ||

He states the true nature of debate (*vādatattva*) with the words "of the teacher and the pupil," and so forth. The meaning is that this is called "debate" (*vāda*) by those who know it; which one? He says: "the cause for the practice of discourse. Discourse (*kathā*) is that which is based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); its practice is the cause [of proficiency]. Of whom? Of the teacher and the pupil. The teacher (*ācārya*) is the preceptor (*guru*), the instructor (*adhyāpaka*); and the pupil (*śiṣya*) is to be understood as the student (*adhyetṛ*). Why? Because of the adoption of a position and a counter-position (*pakṣapratipakṣaparigrahāt*). A position (*pakṣa*) is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). The pupil is to be understood as the student. Why? Because of the adoption of a position and a counter-position; a position is the prima facie argument.

The acceptance of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, as well as the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*), which is the subsequent position (*uttarapakṣa*) characterized by proficiency in presenting refutations against the thesis and other elements employed by the proponent of the prior position (*pūrvapakṣavādin*); the meaning is "by the acceptance" or "by the inclusion" of these two. The Teacher (*ācārya*) accepts the prior position and explains it, while the student (*śiṣya*) adopts the subsequent position and refutes the prior position. Thus, for the sake of practice, independently of defeat or victory, or of points of defeat such as quibbling (*chala*) and futile rejoinders (*jāti*), that assembly where the teacher and student engage in discussion by accepting a position and its counter-position is to be known as *vāda*. || 29 ||
That debate which seeks victory and employs refutations such as quibbling (chala) and futile rejoinders (jāti) is called *jalpa*;
that same *jalpa*, when devoid of a counter-position (*pratipakṣa*), is *vitaṇḍā*.

Now he states its specific distinction: "the debate of those seeking victory" (*vijigīṣukathā*). The connection is that this is *jalpa*. This refers to the employment of fallacies such as *chala* and *jāti* when there exists a discussion initiated by a proponent and an opponent desiring victory through the presentation of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). *Chala* is of three kinds: verbal quibble (*vākchala*), general quibble (*sāmānyacchala*), and figurative quibble (*upacāracchala*).

The "types" (*jāti*) consist of twenty-four varieties; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) and so forth are included. By means of these, "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*) consists in generating a web of refutations against the position (*pakṣa*) and other elements proposed by an opponent and then eliminating them. Furthermore, it involves the production of refutations against an opponent's argument through the employment of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and so on, for the purpose of establishing one's own desired position as a means of attaining the true path. As it has been said: "How else could those whose mouths are set in motion by fragments of ill-taught, fallacious reasoning, and who are adorned with the faults of destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*), be conquered?"
"The world follows what it has previously followed and is thus deceived onto a wrong path;
thinking 'let it not go [there],' the compassionate Sage spoke of [the use of] deception and the like. Thus [it is said].

When a crisis or an urgent occasion arises, the establishment of one's own position even by means of quibbles (*chala*) and the like is permitted; for in the victory of an opponent, there is the possibility of faults such as the destruction of the Dharma. Therefore, victory even by means of quibbles is preferable. Thus, "devoid of a counter-position" (*pratipakṣarahita*) means lacking the proof of a counter-thesis; this refers to the *vaitaṇḍika*, who, not establishing a position of his own, merely refutes what is said by the other through whatever arguments he may employ. || 30 ||

Fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) include the unestablished (asiddha) and so forth; quibble (chala) is as in "the well has new water"; and futile rejoinders (jāti) are fallacious refutations (dūṣaṇābhāsa), those by which the thesis (pakṣa) and other elements are not truly refuted. (31)

"Pseudo-reasons (hetvābhāsas) are to be known. Which are they? He says: "The unestablished and so forth"—the five pseudo-reasons, namely the unestablished (asiddha), the contradictory (viruddha), the inconclusive (anaikāntika), the mistimed (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), and the counter-balanced (prakaraṇasama), are to be known. Among these, that which lacks the property of being present in the subject (pakṣa) is the unestablished; that which exists in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) and does not exist in the similar instances (sapakṣa) is the contradictory; that which occurs in all three [subject, similar, and dissimilar] instances is the inconclusive; that which occurs in a subject that contradicts perception, inference, or scripture is the mistimed; and that which is employed as a reason while failing to apprehend a distinguishing feature is the counter-balanced. The examples are to be inferred by oneself.

"Quibble" (*chala*) is the subversion of a statement by imagining a meaning other than that intended by the opponent in their proposition. To explain how this occurs: when a proponent uses the word "new" (*nava*) in the discourse "The well has new water" (*kūpo navodakaḥ*) with the sense of expressing something recently acquired, the quibbler superimposes the numerical value "nine" (*nava*) upon it and refutes it, saying, "How can there be nine measures of water in a single well? This is "verbal quibble" (*vāk-chala*). He also mentions the remaining two types of quibble as they arise in the context: even those that lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅgin*) through mere possibility (*sambhāvanā*).

The quibble regarding the genus (*sāmānyacchalam*) is the denial [of a statement] by superimposing upon it the status of being a cause for the genus. For example, in the context of praising a Brahmin—someone saying, "Oh, what a Brahmin he is, endowed with learning and conduct"—another person who employs this quibble, superimposing the status of being a cause upon *brāhmaṇatva* (the state of being a Brahmin), challenges him while refuting: "If the endowment of learning and conduct exists in a Brahmin, then it would also exist in a *vrātya*; for even a *vrātya* is indeed a Brahmin."

Quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāracchala*) is the opposition raised by denying the primary sense when a figurative application has been made; for example, when it is said, "The platforms are crying out," another person opposes this by asking, "How can inanimate platforms cry out? Thus should the nature of the three types of quibble be understood.

"Jātayaḥ," and so forth. *Jātis* (futile rejoinders) are semblances of refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsas*). They are called "semblances of refutations" because, although they are not actual refutations, they appear as such. By means of these, the thesis (*pakṣa*) and other elements are not truly refuted; since they are mere semblances, a flaw in the thesis cannot be successfully brought forward. Rather, when a valid reason (*hetu*) or a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) has been employed by the proponent, a *jāti* is a counter-position (*pratyavasthāna*) consisting primarily of a reflection upon the reason, employed when the flaw of that [reason] does not immediately appear. This [jāti] has twenty-four divisions based on the distinctions in counter-positions such as similarity (*sādharmya*) and so forth. Among these, a counter-position based on similarity is the *jāti* known as *sādharmyasamā*.

When the argument has been stated as "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar," the counter-argument based on similarity (*sādharmya*) is as follows: "If sound is impermanent due to its similarity to the impermanent jar by virtue of being produced, then it must also be permanent due to its similarity to the permanent ether (*ākāśa*) by virtue of being incorporeal. Counter-argument based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is the fallacy known as *vaidharmyasama*. When the same aforementioned argument has been stated by way of dissimilarity—namely, "Sound is permanent because it is incorporeal; for that which is corporeal is impermanent, such as a jar and the like"—the counter-argument based on dissimilarity is as follows: [if it were so]. This is the fallacy of *vaidharmyasama*.

For if sound is impermanent because it is produced and thus possesses the dissimilarity to eternal space, then it would follow that it is eternal because it is incorporeal and thus possesses the dissimilarity to impermanent things such as jars, since there is no distinction between the two cases.

The two fallacies known as *utkarṣasama* (balancing the addition) and *apakarṣasama* (balancing the subtraction) consist in counter-objection by means of addition and subtraction. In that same argument, one employs the *utkarṣasama* fallacy by attributing some property of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharma*) to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). For instance: "If sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot, then it must also be corporeal, just like a pot; if it were not corporeal, then let it not be impermanent either, like a pot. In this way, one attributes the addition of another property (*dharmāntarotkarṣa*) to the sound. As for subtraction (*apakarṣa*), however: "A pot is produced, yet it is not audible..."
If it were seen that sound is likewise [eternal], then one would not remove the property of audibility from sound, lest it too—like a pot—be non-eternal.

The two *jātis* (futile rejoinders) known as *varṇyasama* and *avarṇyasama* consist in counter-objections based on the "probandum" (*varṇya*) and the "non-probandum" (*avarṇya*). That which is to be demonstrated is the *varṇya*, and its opposite is the *avarṇya*. One employs these two *jātis*, *varṇyasama* and *avarṇyasama*, by reversing the properties of the probandum and the example; for instance, one argues that the property of sound, such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), is not like the property of a jar, and the property of a jar is not like the property of sound. For indeed, the property of the probandum and the property of the example must be made equivalent.

In this case, however, there is a reversal: for the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth that belongs to a jar is not the same as that which belongs to sound; for the "producedness" of a jar is of one kind, being generated by a potter and the like, whereas that of sound is born from the operation of the palate, lips, and so on. The fallacy of "balancing the alternative" (*vikalpasamā jātiḥ*) is an objection raised by means of an alternative regarding another property. For example: some produced things are seen to be soft, such as a bed of wool (*rāṅkavaśayyā*), while others are hard, such as an axe; likewise, some produced things will be impermanent, such as a jar, while others will be permanent, such as sound.

The *sādhyasamā* (balancing the probandum) sophistry consists in opposing an argument by establishing an equality with the probandum (*sādhya*). For example: "If it follows that as the jar is, so is the sound; then as the sound is, so is the jar. Since the sound is the probandum, the jar would also become a probandum. Consequently, the jar could not serve as an example for the probandum, because it would possess a contradictory characteristic and thus fail to be an example. If this were not the case, even then, due to the difference in nature, it would all the more clearly not be an example.

The *prāptyaprāptisama* (balancing by attainment and non-attainment) is a futile rejoinder that opposes [the argument] through the two alternatives of attainment and non-attainment. For example: "Is this 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*), which you have put forward as a proof, established by attaining the probandum or without attaining it? If it is by attaining, then attainment occurs only between two things that both exist, not between one that exists and one that does not; and since both would exist, what would be the probandum and what the proof? But if it is without attaining, then being a proof is illogical, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."

The *prasangasama* futility is an opposition by means of adducing a consequence; for example, when it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar," the proponent of the futility (*jāti-vādin*) says: "If being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is the proof for impermanence, then what is the proof for that being produced? And what is the proof for that [proof]?"

*Pratidṛṣṭāntasama* (the counter-example fallacy) is an opposition based on a counter-example; for instance, when it is stated, "Sound is non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar," the proponent of the *jāti* says: "Just as a jar is seen to be non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort, so too is the counter-example, space, seen to follow immediately upon effort, since it is perceived immediately after the effort of digging a well. This is not merely an objection based on the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason, because it is an opposition formulated by means of a different method.

The *anutpattisama* (balancing the non-arising) fallacy consists in an objection based on non-origination; for example: "In what place could the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) reside, since the subject (*dharmin*) called 'sound' has not yet arisen? Therefore, due to the absence of the reason (*hetu*), the impermanence [of sound] is unestablished. The *sādharmyasama* (balancing the similarity) or *vaidharmyasama* (balancing the dissimilarity) fallacies are those which were previously illustrated; when these same arguments are concluded with a doubt, they become the *saṃśayasama* (balancing the doubt) fallacy. For example: "Is sound impermanent because of its similarity to a jar through the property of being produced, or is it permanent because of its dissimilarity to that [jar] through its similarity to space by virtue of being partless?"

When that same *jāti*—whether it be *sādharmyasama* or *vaidharmyasama*—is employed with the intention of raising a second alternative, it becomes *prakaraṇasama*. In the very same application, such as "sound is non-eternal because it is produced, like a jar," or "sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound" (*śabdatva*), one should understand the distinction [between these types] to exist merely through the difference in the manner of their presentation.

The *ahetusamā* (the "equal to a non-reason") sophistical refutation consists in opposing a reason by asserting that its existence at any of the three times is untenable; for instance: if the reason is the means of proof (*sādhana*), it must exist either before, after, or simultaneously with that which is to be proven (*sādhya*). If it exists before, then since the *sādhya* is non-existent, of what would it be the means of proof? If the means of proof exists later, then the *sādhya* already exists beforehand, and if that is already established, what is the use of a means of proof? If the *sādhya* and the *sādhana* exist simultaneously, then—just like the left and right horns of a cow—the relationship of *sādhya* and *sādhana* could not possibly exist between them.

The *jāti* (futile rejoinder) called *arthāpatti* (presumption) consists in opposing an argument by means of presumption. For instance, if it is argued that "sound is impermanent because of its similarity to the impermanent, namely its being produced," one might object: "By implication (*arthāt*), it follows that sound must be permanent because of its similarity to the permanent; and indeed, it possesses a similarity with the permanent ether (*ākāśa*), namely, partlessness. This is merely a specific mode of raising an objection.

The *aviśeṣasamā* (balancing through non-difference) fallacy consists in an objection raised by establishing a lack of distinction; for example: "If it is admitted that sound and a jar share one common property, namely 'being produced,' then, due to their connection with that same property, there would be no distinction between them. Consequently, it follows that all things would likewise be without distinction."

The *upapattisama* fallacy is an objection based on a logical justification (*upapatti*). For example: "If the impermanence of sound is established by the justification of its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), why does its permanence not also follow from the justification of its being partless (*niravayavatva*)? Since both positions are equally justified, the result is indecision. This is merely a different mode of pointing out the flaw, intended to show that the conclusion remains unsettled due to the justification for both sides.

The *jāti* (futile rejoinder) called "balancing the apprehension" (*upalabdhisama*) consists in an objection based on what is apprehended. For example, when it is argued that "sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort," one objects: "Indeed, following immediately upon effort is not the proof for impermanence; that is called a 'proof' by which the probandum cannot be apprehended without it. Yet, impermanence is apprehended even without [following] immediately upon effort, as in the case of lightning and the like; and so it is also in the case of sound in certain instances, such as when it is produced by trees being broken by the force of the wind."

The "balancing by non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhisama*) fallacy occurs due to the counter-objection based on non-apprehension. For example, when that very same reason—"being produced immediately after effort"—has been put forward, the proponent of the fallacy says: "Sound is not an effect of effort; it already exists prior to its utterance, but it is not perceived because of the presence of an obstruction. If it is argued, "Even though the obstruction is not perceived, since [the sound] is not perceived, it simply does not exist," [the reply is]: No, because even when the obstruction is not perceived, the non-perception [of the sound] still persists; and since there is no perception of the non-apprehension of the obstruction, that [non-apprehension] is absent. In the absence of that...

Because an obstruction is perceived, the existence [of sound] follows; therefore, just as in the case of water behind a root-stake that is itself obstructed, the non-perception of sound prior to its utterance is caused solely by the perception of an obstruction. Thus, since there is no effect produced by effort, sound is eternal.

The *nityasamā* (balancing the eternal) fallacy consists in establishing the eternity of sound by means of an alternative between the permanence or impermanence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). For example, when it is proposed that "sound is impermanent," the proponent of the fallacy (*jātivādī*) makes a distinction: "Is this impermanence attributed to sound itself impermanent or permanent? If it is impermanent, then it must necessarily pass away; thus, due to the absence of impermanence, sound would be eternal. On the other hand, if it is indeed permanent, then because a property (*dharma*) cannot exist without a substratum (*āśraya*), the very substratum of that [impermanence] must be eternal.
If it is argued that sound, too, is indeed eternal, we say no; for if it were non-eternal, it would be impossible for its property (to be eternal). Thus, in both ways, sound is eternal.

Thus, the *jāti* (futile rejoinder) called "the equalization of the non-eternal" (*anityasamā*) consists in an objection raised by establishing the non-eternality of all things. For example, [one might argue]: "Since sound possesses the common property of non-eternality with a jar, if its non-eternality is established, then because there is some common property with a jar for all objects whatsoever, they too would have to be non-eternal. Or, if other objects do not become non-eternal despite having such a state, then let it be that sound does not either. This *jāti* is distinct from "the equalization of the indistinguishable" (*aviśeṣasamā*), because it proceeds by first establishing mere non-eternality and then pointing out the lack of distinction [between the case at hand and others].

The *kāryasama* (equal-to-the-effect) fallacy is an objection raised by pointing out the diversity of effects produced by effort. For example, when it is stated, "Sound is non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort," the proponent of the fallacy says: "Two types of effects are observed regarding effort: some are produced while being previously non-existent, such as a jar and the like; others are manifested while already existing through the removal of an obstruction, such as a tree-root or a peg hidden within the earth."

Thus, because there is a diversity regarding whether sound is manifested or produced by effort due to the difference between effort and its effect, a doubt arises as to whether "sound is manifested or produced by effort. Furthermore, the *kāryasama* (balancing the effect) fallacy differs from the *saṃśayasama* (balancing the doubt) because of the difference in the ways in which the doubt is introduced.

Therefore, although the *jātis* (futilities) are infinite due to the differences in the options for the objects of their presentation, these twenty-four varieties of *jāti* have been shown here with the intention of providing mixed examples. || 31 ||

The points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) have been declared as those by which an opponent is defeated, consisting of various divisions such as the abandonment of a thesis, its renunciation, contradiction, and so forth. || 32 ||

Having discussed fallacious refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*), he states the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) with the words beginning "the point of defeat" (*nigrahasthānam*). That by which the opponent, the adversary, is defeated—that is, the proponent of another view is cast into a state of verbal defeat—is called or described as a "point of defeat. Indicating some of its varieties by name, he says: "possessing divisions such as abandonment of the thesis, renunciation, and contradiction. Here, "abandonment," "renunciation," and "contradiction" are connected with the word "thesis" (*pratijñā*); by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he refers to the remaining varieties as well. That by which this web of refutations is produced is a "point of defeat."

As it has been stated: "Misconception and non-comprehension are the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Among these, misconception consists of the notion that something is a proof when it is a fallacy of proof, and the notion that something is a refutation when it is a fallacy of refutation. Non-comprehension consists of failing to refute a proof and failing to rescue a refutation. These points of defeat are of twenty-two kinds, as follows: abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*), shifting the proposition (*pratijñāntara*), contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*), renouncing the proposition (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*), shifting the reason (*hetvantara*), and shifting the subject matter (*arthāntara*).

Meaningless, unintelligible, irrelevant, mistimed, deficient, redundant, repetitive, failure to restate, lack of understanding, lack of ingenuity, distraction, admission of one's own position, neglect of what should be censured, censuring what should not be censured, deviation from a tenet, and fallacious reasons.

In that case, when the reason has been rendered inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for one who accepts the property of the counter-example within their own example, there occurs the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "Abandonment of the Proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*). For instance, when a proponent states "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a pot" in order to prove his proposition, and the opponent renders the reason inconclusive by pointing out that "the universal (*sāmānya*), though perceptible by the senses, is seen to be eternal," if the proponent should then say, "If that is so, then the pot must also be eternal like the universal," he who speaks thus abandons his proposition that sound is impermanent.

When an opponent has refuted the meaning of a proposition, for one who then asserts the proof of another property regarding that very same subject, it constitutes the point of defeat called "shifting the proposition" (*pratijñāntara*). For example, when it has been stated, "Sound is non-eternal because it is perceptible by the senses," and the opponent has pointed out the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of the universal (*sāmānya*), if one should say, "It is correct that the universal is perceptible and eternal, for it is all-pervading, whereas sound is not all-pervading," this [latter statement] is distinct from the original proposition, "Sound is non-eternal."
A change of proposition (*pratijñāntara*) occurs when one is defeated by a different proposition, such as "sound is not all-pervading.

Contradiction between the proposition and the reason (*pratijñāhetuvirodha*) is the point of defeat known as "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodha*).
