For example: "Substance is distinct from its qualities, because no object other than [the qualities] such as color is perceived. This is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason: if substance is distinct from its qualities, how can there be a non-perception of any object other than color and the rest? Conversely, if there is a non-perception of any object other than color and the rest, how can substance be distinct from its qualities? Thus, this is...

One is defeated by stating contradictory propositions regarding the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*). When the proof of one's own position has been refuted by an opponent and one is unable to rescue it, the point of defeat called "renunciation" (*pratisaṃnyāsa*) occurs when one withdraws the very thesis. For example, when it has been stated that "sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of that reason has been pointed out by the opponent on the grounds of its presence in the universal (*sāmānya*), if one should say, "Who said that sound is permanent?"—then, due to this renunciation of the thesis, one becomes defeated.

When a reason has been stated without qualification and that reason has been refuted, for one who then states a qualification for it, there occurs the point of defeat called "another reason" (*hetvantara*). In that very same argument, while the general [reason] has already been shown to be fallacious due to its deviation (*vyabhicāra*), one who employs a qualification such as "provided that it possesses the nature of being a genus" becomes defeated by means of another reason.

The *nigrahasthāna* (point of defeat) called "irrelevancy" (*arthāntara*) occurs when one states something different from the subject at hand, even if it is somehow relevant to it. For example, having stated the reason "sound is eternal because it is produced," and then—having introduced the topic that "a reason is a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix derived from the root *hi* with the suffix *tu*, and a word consists of nouns, secondary derivatives, particles, and prefixes"—one proceeds to explain nouns and so forth, thereby being defeated by way of irrelevance.

The mere employment of a sequence of phonemes devoid of a denotable meaning constitutes the point of defeat known as "meaningless naming" (*nirarthaka-nigrahasthāna*). For example, the statement "Sound is eternal because *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa* possess *ga-ja-ḍa-da-ba*, like *gha-jha-ḍha-dha-bha-va-da*" would also result in defeat, either because it is entirely devoid of meaning or because it is useless for the proof of the thesis. Furthermore, when a statement of proof or a statement of refutation, though uttered three times, cannot be understood by the assembly and the opponent, that constitutes the point of defeat known as "unintelligible meaning" (*avijñātārtha-nigrahasthāna*).

The defeat condition known as "the meaningless" (*apārthaka*) occurs when a collection of words is employed that lacks coherence between preceding and succeeding parts, such that the meaning of the sentence remains unestablished, for example: "Ten pomegranates, six cakes."

An inferential statement (*anumānavākya*) that is employed by transposing its members, thereby violating the proper sequence of the proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*), constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "untimeliness" (*aprāptakāla*), because it deviates from the sequence of the inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) required to produce understanding in another, just as one's own internal realization does. Furthermore, when a five-membered statement ought to be employed, if it is deficient by even a single member of the inference, it constitutes the point of defeat known as "deficiency" (*nyūna*), because there is no establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the absence of the means of proof (*sādhana*), and since all five members—beginning with the proposition—are indeed means of proof.

When a matter has already been established by means of a single reason or example, for one to state another reason or another example constitutes the point of defeat known as "redundancy" (*adhika*). Furthermore, the repetition of words or meanings constitutes the point of defeat known as "repetition" (*punarukta*), except in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*). Repetition of words occurs when that very same word is uttered again, such as: "Sound is eternal; sound is eternal. Repetition of meaning, however, occurs when that same meaning is first expressed by one word [and then repeated].

Furthermore, it is stated by way of another synonym: for example, "sound is impermanent" and "the resonance is perishable. However, in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), repetition is not a fault; as in the definition of the conclusion (*nigamana*): "the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the instruction of the reason (*hetu*). On the other hand, when something has been made known to the assembly and even uttered by the disputants, the failure to restate it constitutes the ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "non-reproduction" (*ananubhāṣaṇa*).

Even when the meaning of the opponent's statement has been understood by the assembly, the opponent's lack of knowledge regarding it constitutes the point of defeat called "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). For how could one who does not know the subject matter of the reply provide a reply? Nor is this the same as "non-reproduction" (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), because even when the matter is known, one may be observed to lack the capacity to reproduce it. When the opponent's position has been grasped and reproduced, the failure to perceive a reply to it constitutes the point of defeat called "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*).

The interruption of a discussion due to preoccupation with other business is the point of defeat known as *vikṣepa* (distraction). Having determined that the matter one intends to prove is impossible to establish, one interrupts the discussion by saying, "This duty of mine is being neglected," or "My throat is choked by a cold," and so forth; by thus interrupting the discussion through distraction, one is defeated.

When one fails to remove a fault alleged against one's own position and instead attributes that very same fault to the opponent's position, it constitutes the point of defeat known as *matānujñā* (admission of the opponent's view). For example, when it is said, "You are a thief because you are a human being, like a well-known thief," if one replies, "You too are a thief because you are a human being," one is defeated by *matānujñā*, for by so saying, one has accepted the fault of being a thief as alleged against oneself by the opponent.

The failure to censure one who has reached a point of defeat constitutes the ground for defeat known as *paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa* (neglecting the censurable). One who is "censurable" (*paryanuyojya*) is one who must necessarily be challenged because a ground for defeat has occurred; he is to be addressed with the words, "This ground of defeat has come upon you; therefore, you are defeated. He who overlooks such a person and does not censure them is himself defeated by the neglect of the censurable.

The point of defeat called "charging with what is not a point of defeat" (niranuyojyānuyoga) occurs when one challenges someone who is not in a state of defeat as being in a state of defeat. If one says to a speaker who has argued correctly and without negligence, "You are defeated," even though that person does not deserve defeat, then that challenger himself is defeated for raising a fault that did not exist.

The "departure from a tenet" (*apasiddhānta*) is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) consisting of engaging in a discussion while being bound by a specific tenet; that is, one who first accepts a certain tenet and then commences a discussion, yet in the course of it, states something contrary to that tenet in order to prove the point he wishes to establish or to censure his opponent, is defeated by that very departure from his tenet. Furthermore, the fallacies of reason (*hetvābhāsa*)—such as the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and so forth, as previously described—are also points of defeat. Although there is an infinity of further subdivisions, twenty-two root types of points of defeat have been set forth. || 32 ||
Thus has the summary of the Naiyāyika doctrine been stated; now this [summary] of the categories favored by the Sāṅkhya is being set forth. (33)

Then, concluding [the section], he says: "In this way, of the Naiyāyika doctrine," and so forth. "In this way" (*evam*) means by this method; the summary (*samāsa*), that is, the concise exposition of the Naiyāyika doctrine, which is the teaching of Śiva, has now been told—that is, it has just been presented and is now finalized. Now, however, this summary of the categories (*bhāva*) favored by the Sāṃkhyas is being stated. "Sāṃkhyas" means the followers of Kapila. The meaning is: the summary of those categories favored by them—such as the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) and so on—is being told hereafter. (33)
Some Sāṃkhyas are atheistic, while others have Īśvara as their deity;
for all of them, however, the number of principles (tattvas) remains twenty-five.
He states the nature of their philosophical view with the words beginning "The Sāṅkhyas":

some Sāṅkhyas are atheistic (*nirīśvara*), meaning they do not accept a Lord as a deity, being knowers of the purely spiritual alone; others, however, declare Maheśvara to be the Lord-deity, the presiding authority over their own teaching—this applies to "all" of them. In the doctrine of all these followers of the Sāṅkhya system, whether they maintain that the self is purely eternal or whether they accept a Lord as deity, there are twenty-five principles (*tattvas*). For it is a consensus among all disputants that a principle is indeed the seed that accomplishes liberation (*apavarga*). As it has been said:
One who knows the twenty-five principles is liberated, regardless of which stage of life he follows—whether he has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot; of this there is no doubt.
In his view, the meaning is that there are twenty-five principles (tattvas). || 34 ||
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these three qualities (guṇas) are to be known;
they are characterized respectively by their effects, such as clarity, contentment, and dejection. (35)

He states the three qualities with the words beginning "sattva" and so forth. The word "tāvat" (first/initially) indicates the commencement; thus, the triad of qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—is to be known. That triad of qualities, in its respective order, produces these three signs as effects characterized by clarity, agitation, and dejection. The meaning is that the sign characterized by the effect of clarity arises from the quality of *sattva*—that is, clarity of the face, eyes, and so forth, occurs through the quality of *sattva*.

The meaning is that satisfaction arises from the quality of *rajas*, and that is synonymous with bliss; its signs, such as mental effulgence (*sphūrti*) and so forth, are manifested by the quality of *rajas*. Furthermore, dejection is produced by the quality of *tamas*; dejection—manifested by such things as a lack of luster in the face and contraction of the eyes when one says, "Alas, Fate! I am ruined! I am deceived!"—is the sign of the quality of *tamas*. By the word "dejection and so forth" (*dainyādi*), the threefold suffering (*duḥkhatraya*) is implied, namely: the internal (*ādhyātmika*), the external (*ādhibhautika*), and the celestial (*ādhidaivika*).

Among these, internal suffering (*ādhyātmika*) is of two kinds: physical and mental. Physical suffering is caused by the imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*); mental suffering is based on desire, anger, greed, delusion, envy, and the perception of objects [of sense]. All this is called internal suffering because it is to be remedied by internal means. External suffering to be remedied by external means is twofold: pertaining to other beings (*ādhibhautika*) and pertaining to divine agencies (*ādhidaivika*). Among these, suffering pertaining to other beings has its cause in humans, domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and immobile things; that pertaining to divine agencies has its cause in possession by *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, planetary spirits (*graha*), and so forth. || 35 ||
The state of equilibrium of these [qualities] is indeed called *prakṛti*;
it is denoted by the terms *pradhāna* and *avyakta*, and its nature is eternal. (36)
He states this very point with the words beginning "of these":

"Of these Sāṃkhyas, that which is the state of equilibrium—the equal abiding—of the three qualities, namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which consist respectively of pleasure, pain, and dejection, and possess the properties of buoyancy, excitation, and heaviness; that indeed is called *prakṛti*. The word "indeed" (*kila*) refers to traditional authoritative report; that *prakṛti* is so described, and furthermore, it is denoted by the terms *pradhāna* and *avyakta*, and by the terms *pradhāna* and *avyakta*, *prakṛti* is designated.

In the treatise (*śāstra*), *prakṛti*, *pradhāna*, and *avyakta* are synonyms; the meaning is that they are not distinct principles. Likewise, it is established as having an eternal nature (*nityasvarūpikā*) by virtue of its perpetual state of being (*śāśvatabhāvanatayā*). And it is said to be eternal and the locus of manifold individual spirits (*puruṣa*). According to the vision of that [system], *prakṛti* says: "Therefore, no one at all is truly bound, nor liberated, nor does he transmigrate. It is *prakṛti*, which has manifold loci, that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated. (36) Thus it is said.
From that, the intellect (buddhi) is produced, which is called the "Great One" (mahat);
from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) arises, and from that, the group of sixteen. || 37 ||
In one afflicted by these three kinds of suffering, a desire to know [the truth] arises; therefore, he states those very principles with the words beginning "therefore" (tataḥ).

From those three *guṇas*, the intellect (*buddhi*) is born—that which is called "the Great" (*mahān*), meaning it is celebrated by the term "the Great. It is thus and not otherwise: "This is a cow, not a horse; this is a post, not a person. Such is the determination (*adhyavasāya*). That determination which is the cause for the comprehension of objects is the intellect. Its forms are eight, well-known from that [Sāṃkhya] philosophy, as it has been said: the four forms consisting of virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) are *sāttvika*; whereas those beginning with non-virtue (*adharma*)...

The four qualities that serve as its opposites are the *tāmasa* ones; thus there are eight. From that intellect (*buddhi*) arises the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). It consists of self-conceit (*abhimāna*), taking the form of such cognitions as: "I am in sound," "I am in form," "I am in taste," "I am in touch," "I am in smell," "I am the master," "I am the lord," "this one has been killed by me," and "I shall kill you. From that ego-sense, the group of sixteen is born—this is to be supplied [as the verb], just as in the case of [the verbs] "there is" (*asti*) or "it exists" (*bhavati*). These are the five sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) and the five organs of action (*karmendriya*).

The eleventh is the mind; together with the five elements, this constitutes the group of sixteen. Thus said Īśvarakṛṣṇa: "Root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and modification;
the group of sixteen is modification only; and the person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor modification. (SK 3.37)
Touching, tasting, smelling, seeing, and hearing as the fifth—these they call the five organs of perception (buddhīndriya), as well as the organs of action (karmendriya). || 38 ||
The anus, the generative organ, speech, the hands, and the feet, as well as the mind, along with the other five subtle elements (tanmātras), constitute the sixteen [evolutes]. (39)
He states the group of sixteen itself with the words beginning "touching" (*sparśanam*).

The connection is that there are five sense organs (*buddhīndriyāṇi*). Touching is the organ of the skin; tasting is the tongue; smelling is the nose; sight is the eye; and the fifth is hearing, which is the ear. These five, being primarily characterized by cognition and arising as companions to cognition, produce knowledge; therefore, those who hold that view call them "sense organs" (*buddhīndriyāṇi*). Likewise, there are the "organs of action" (*karmendriyāṇi*).

Likewise, he refers to the mere number five previously mentioned and states those very things: "known as the anus, the generative organ, speech, the hands, and the feet. The anus is *apāna*; the generative organ (*upastha*) is the organ of procreation; speech is *vāk* (the faculty of speech); the hand is the arm; and the foot is the limb. These five are the organs of action (*karmendriyas*). Action (*karman*) is the activity of performing an effect; the organs that are the instruments (*sādhana*) for that are the organs of action. Similarly, the meaning is that the mind (*manas*) is the eleventh organ. Furthermore, there are the five forms of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), known as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Thus, these sixteen are to be known. (38–39)
From form comes fire, from taste comes water, from smell comes earth, and from sound comes ether;
likewise, from touch comes air—thus from these five [qualities] arise the five elements.
He states the production of the five gross elements from the five subtle elements (tanmātras) with the words "from form, fire," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "from the five": the connection is that the group of five gross elements arises from the five subtle elements; from the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*) comes fire; from the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*) comes water; from the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) comes earth; from the subtle element of sound (*svaratanmātra*) comes space; and from the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*) comes air. Thus, the five gross elements are produced from the five subtle elements. This is a statement of their respective unique qualities: the production [is such that] from the subtle element of sound comes space, which has sound as its quality, for sound is the quality of the ether (*ambara*).

From the *sparśatanmātra* (subtle element of touch) accompanied by the *śabdatanmātra* (subtle element of sound), air (*vāyu*) arises, possessing the qualities of sound and touch; from the *rūpatanmātra* (subtle element of form) accompanied by the *śabdatanmātra* and *sparśatanmātra*, fire (*tejas*) arises, possessing the qualities of sound, touch, and form; from the *rasatanmātra* (subtle element of taste) accompanied by the *śabdatanmātra*, *sparśatanmātra*, and *rūpatanmātra*, water (*āpaḥ*) arises, possessing the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste; [and] from the *gandhatanmātra* (subtle element of smell) accompanied by the *śabdatanmātra*, *sparśatanmātra*, *rūpatanmātra*, and *rasatanmātra*.
The earth is born possessing the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; the meaning is that from the five [subtle elements] arise the five gross elements. || 40 ||
Thus, in the Sāṃkhya system, the Pradhāna has been described as consisting of twenty-four principles.
But the other [principle], the Puruṣa, is accepted as the eternal conscious reality—the non-agent, devoid of qualities, yet the enjoyer. (41)
Concluding the detailed exposition of *prakṛti*, he says "evam" and so forth.

In this manner, by the method previously described, the *pradhāna*—consisting of twenty-four principles (*tattva*)—is presented according to the Sāṃkhya system. The meaning is that *prakṛti* has been described as having the following form: the triad of *prakṛti*, *mahat*, and *ahaṅkāra*; the five sense organs (*buddhīndriya*); the five organs of action (*karmendriya*); the single mind (*manas*); the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); and the five gross elements (*bhūta*). He states the twenty-fifth principle with the words "anyastu."

The Puruṣa is another, being a non-agent, because the properties such as transmigratory existence belong to Prakṛti alone. As it has been said: "Prakṛti acts; Prakṛti is bound; Prakṛti is released. The Puruṣa is unbound; the Puruṣa is liberated; the Puruṣa indeed—formless, conscious, the enjoyer, eternal, omnipresent, inactive, a non-agent, devoid of qualities, and subtle—is the Self in the Sāṃkhya philosophy."

He states the qualities of the Puruṣa: "devoid of qualities" (viguṇa). This means he is devoid of the three qualities consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas; likewise, he is the enjoyer (bhoktā), the experiencer. Such is the Person (pumān), the twenty-fifth principle (tattva)—this is the meaning.

Likewise, it is "endowed with eternal consciousness" (*nityacidabhyupeta*); that is, it is accompanied by and possessed of that which is both eternal and consciousness—the power of sentience (*caitanya-śakti*). For the Self (*ātman*) considers itself to be non-different from the intellect (*buddhi*). Objects such as pleasure and pain enter the intellect through the gateway of the senses. And the intellect has the form of a mirror with two faces; therefore, the power of sentience is reflected in it. Consequently, one metaphorically designates oneself as "I am happy" or "I am suffering. As it is said in the *Pātañjala*: "Even though the Puruṣa is pure, [it perceives] the cognition..."

"One perceives the intellect; perceiving it, although not of its nature, one appears as if having that as one's nature. But in the primary sense, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is devoid of the determination of objects, because it is the intellect alone that has the nature of determining objects. Furthermore, due to the proximity of the power of consciousness, the intellect, though insentient, appears as if it were sentient. As the *Vādamahārṇava* also says: "The reflection of the object, transferred to the mirror of the intellect, ascends into the *puruṣa*, which is like a second mirror."

That alone constitutes its state of being an enjoyer, and not the production of a modification. Thus says Āsuri: "The experience of this [Self] is said to occur when the intellect has been transformed by the pure Seer, like the clear reflection of the moon arising in water."
Vindhyavāsin, however, explains experience in this way:
"The Spirit, whose nature is indeed unchanging,
causes the insentient mind to manifest its own likeness through the proximity of the limiting adjunct (upādhi), just as a crystal [reflects the color of a nearby object]."
Thus, [the Self] is endowed with eternal, conscious knowledge.

Although bondage, liberation, and transmigratory existence belong to the eternal Self, they are metaphorically attributed to it—just as victory and defeat, though occurring among the servants, are figuratively applied to the master due to his connection with the results such as gain or loss—so too here; thus there is no fault. || 41 ||
Thus, for the Sāṃkhya, there are twenty-five principles;
and here, the interaction between primordial matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa) is like that of the lame man and the blind man.

He states the summary of the principles with the verse beginning "By the system of twenty-five principles," and so forth. The first half [of the verse] is self-evident. Here, in the Sāṃkhya system, the "functioning" (*vṛtti*) or operation of *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and *nara* (the person)—that is, *prakṛti* (nature) and *puruṣa* (the self)—is like that of the lame man and the blind man. The lame man is one deprived of feet, and the blind man is one deprived of eyes. Just as the lame man and the blind man, only when joined together, are capable of accomplishing a task and not when separated, so too is the agency for the performance of action shared by *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. The meaning is that the *puruṣa* experiences what has been acquired by *prakṛti*. || 42 ||

Liberation is the disjunction from primordial nature (prakṛti) resulting solely from the internal knowledge of the Puruṣa. Furthermore, there are three means of valid cognition: perception, inference, and verbal testimony. || 43 ||

He states the measure of liberation with the words "separation from *prakṛti*," and so forth. To the question "What is called liberation? he replies: liberation is that separation of the *puruṣa*, the self, from *prakṛti*, which occurs through the cutting of the various bonds resulting from internal knowledge. When there is separation—that is, a dissociation—from *prakṛti*, there is the final emancipation (*apavarga*) of the *puruṣa*. Furthermore, internal knowledge arises from the cutting of the bonds; and the bond is threefold, distinguished as being of the nature of *prakṛti*, of transformation (*vaikṛtika*), and of ritual action (*dākṣiṇa*).

For example: through knowledge of the Self regarding primordial nature (*prakṛti*), those who worship primordial nature undergo bondage pertaining to *prakṛti*. Those who, by means of the intellect of the Puruṣa, worship only the transformations—namely the elements, the senses, the ego, and the intellect—undergo bondage pertaining to transformation (*vaikārika*). Regarding "sacrificial rites and public works" (*iṣṭāpūrta*): this refers to sacrificial rites, public works, and the giving of food to people; one who performs such rites while ignorant of the principle of the Puruṣa is bound, his mind being afflicted by desire. Thus it is said: "The fools who consider sacrificial rites and public works to be the highest, and who rejoice in nothing else as a means to excellence..."
Having ascended to the back of the firmament by means of their good deeds, they enter this world or one even lower.
Because of this statement [in the scripture]: "The Muni is not born, nor does he die" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.10).

Thus, from the severance of the threefold bondage, there arises the experience of the Puruṣa; thereafter follows the disjunction of the Puruṣa from Prakṛti. And when [the world-process] has ceased due to the discriminative vision of the distinction between Prakṛti and Puruṣa, there may be—indeed, there comes to be—the threefold means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*laiṅgika*), and verbal testimony (*śābda*). The word "and" (*ca*) is connected to every [term]. Perception is that which is apprehended by the senses; inference is that which is accessible through reasoning; and verbal testimony is that which consists of sacred tradition (*āgama*). Thus, there are three means of valid cognition. (43)
[The Jaina view:
Thus, the summary of the Sāṃkhya doctrine has also been stated; now, the concise presentation of the Jaina philosophy, characterized by sound reasoning, is being told. (44)
Now, concluding [the discussion], he says: "Thus" (*evam*).

In the manner previously described, the summary—that is, the concise exposition—of the Sāṃkhya doctrine has also been stated. The word "also" (*api*) serves as a conjunction; it means that not only have the summaries of the Buddhist and Naiyāyika systems been stated, but the summary of the Sāṃkhya doctrine has now been stated as well. The term "Sāṃkhya" is a designation derived from the person [Kapila]; they are called "Sāṃkhyas" because they belong to Saṃkhya. Alternatively, the letter *ś* is palatal (*tālavya*); the first teacher was named Śaṅkha.

Now he states the brief exposition of the Jaina doctrine as it follows in sequence—the word "now" (*adhunā*) connects with the second half of the verse. "Now," that is, at this time, the summary of knowledge and perception (*jñāna-darśana-saṃkṣepa*) is being told. Of what nature is it? It is "possessing excellent discernment" (*suvicāravān*); the suffix *matup* is used in the sense of "that which has an excellent (*su-śobhana*) discernment (*vicāra*) as its object. The term "possessing excellent discernment" is used with specific intent. For other systems of thought hold: "The Purāṇas, the Dharma of Manu, the Veda with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*), and medical science—these four are established by authority (*ājñā-siddha*) and should not be assailed by logical arguments (*hetubhiḥ*)."
By such statements as these, they do not admit [the matter] into the path of critical inquiry. But the Jaina says: "There is something that must be said; therefore, this is not left unexamined.
If gold were truly free from defects, why would it fear testing?"

Thus, as one who has traveled the path of familiarity with a succession of reasoned investigations, the Jaina plunges only into the path of reason; the supreme Arhat does not transgress reason out of partiality for tradition and the like. And it has been said:
"I have no partiality for Vīra, nor hatred for Kapila and others;
one should accept the words of whoever possesses reason."

Thus, because the expansion of opposing views has been refuted by hundreds of arguments and reasons, it should be understood that the application of the unique qualification "possessing thorough discernment" (*suvicāravān*) is established. || 44 ||
The Lord of Jinas is the deity there, free from passion and hatred;
having slain the great wrestler of delusion, he possesses absolute knowledge and vision. || 45 ||
Worshipped by the lords of both gods and asuras, the teacher of the true nature of reality, having brought about the total destruction of all karma, he has attained the supreme state. (46)

He states that very point with the words "the Lord of Jinas is the deity," and so forth. In this context, the connection is as follows: in that Jain doctrine, the Lord of Jinas (jinendra) is the deity who, having brought about the total destruction of karma, has attained the supreme state (*parama-pada*). Regarding the term *jinendra*: those who conquer passion and the like are *jinās*, meaning the ordinary *kevalins*; their lord (*indra*) is the master. Such a Lord of Jinas, endowed with the wealth of thirty-four incomparable excellences (*atiśayas*), is the deity, the founder of the system, the primordial person (*ādipuruṣa*). To answer the question "What kind of one is he who has attained the auspicious state (*śiva*)?", he states the following unique qualifiers: "devoid of attachment and aversion" (*rāga-dveṣa-vivarjita*).

Thus: *rāga* (attachment) is worldly affection characterized by favor; *dveṣa* (aversion) is characterized by hostility resulting from the persistence of dispassion and so forth. He is "devoid" (*vivarjita*) or free from these two. These two alone are well-known in the scriptures as difficult to conquer and as obstacles to liberation, because they are the causes for the onset of endless worldly existence. As it has been said: "Who would suffer misery? Who would not be filled with joy by pleasures?
And who would not attain liberation, were it not for attachment and aversion?"
Who would experience suffering? Who would not be filled with wonder by joys?
And who would not attain liberation, were it not for passion and hatred?

Likewise, he is one by whom the great wrestler of delusion (*mahāmoha*) has been slain. Delusion (*moha*) refers to the bewilderment arising from the fruition of deluding karma (*mohanīyakarma*), such as the desire for liberation even from scriptures characterized by violence; because it is difficult to overcome, it is like a "great wrestler" (*mahāmalla*). He is thus described as one by whom this great wrestler of delusion has been destroyed. Precisely because of the presence of passion, aversion, and delusion, the founders of other sects do not appear as factors conducive to liberation, and the existence of these [passions] among them is indeed easily discerned. As it has been said: "Passion is inferred from attachment to women; aversion is known through the weapons used to strike at enemies."
Delusion is cured by the fault of following false conduct and scriptures; he, the God, for whom this does not exist, is indeed the Arhat.

Thus, the Blessed One is free from attachment, aversion, and delusion; likewise, he possesses *kevalajñāna* (perfect knowledge) and *kevaladarśana* (perfect perception). Knowledge is the specific cognition of individual entities such as the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees, whereas perception is the general cognition of them as "a forest. The word "perfect" (*kevala*) applies to both: it refers to one whose knowledge and perception are perfect, being independent of the senses and other such means. Indeed, the Blessed One consists of perfect knowledge and perfect perception, like a pure pearl resting in the palm of his hand.

The term "omniscient vision" (*kevalajñānadarśana*) is used with specific intent, for it refers to that which perceives this entire world-essence—which is pure in both substance and mode—without interruption. For others, vision arises first and then knowledge; however, for the Omniscient One, knowledge arises first and then vision. He is worthy of worship by the lords of gods and asuras, constantly attended by those diligent in the performance of service, and venerable to the hosts of gods and dānavas who act as his servants; yet, even for one so worthy of worship by such beings, being served by the multitudes of humans, animals, celestial beings, and kinnaras is merely incidental.

Likewise, he teaches the reality of things as they truly are; he teaches that categories of existence consist of infinite attributes (*dharma*), such as substance and mode, permanence and impermanence, generality and particularity, existence and non-existence, expressibility and so forth. For instance—the defining characteristic of a real entity is its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). This is not possible in the case of absolute permanence; for that which is permanent is by nature unchanging, unproduced, and stable in a single form. Would such a thing perform causal efficiency successively or simultaneously? [It could not,] because objects possess mutually distinct attributes.

Because there is no production by way of another mode, it cannot occur successively; for that [efficient cause], being capable, would necessarily perform those actions extending over a period of time at the very moment of the first action, since it is impossible for one who is capable to delay in time. Or, if it does delay in time, its capacity has not been attained. For if you argue that "the capable [cause] performs that effect through the conjunction of its auxiliary conditions," [we reply: no.

No; for its capacity depends on the operation of other auxiliary factors, according to the maxim that "that which is dependent is incapable. If it is argued that it is not the entity itself that requires the auxiliaries, but rather the effect that requires them when the auxiliaries are absent, then we ask: is that entity incapable or capable? If it is capable, why does it require those investigations and so forth regarding the auxiliaries instead of producing the effect immediately?

Now, even though a seed is capable, it produces a sprout only when accompanied by auxiliary factors such as soil, water, and wind, and not otherwise. Therefore, is something conferred upon the seed by these auxiliaries, or not? If nothing is conferred, then why does the seed not remain indifferent toward its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) just as it was before the presence of the auxiliaries? If, on the other hand, something is conferred, then it must be stated whether that benefit produced by them is distinct from or non-distinct from the seed itself. If it is non-distinct, then it is the seed itself that is being produced; thus, for one who desires gain, the destruction of the very root has occurred.

Because it would follow that [the universal] is impermanent due to being produced; and if there were a difference [between the universal and the individual], how could there be assistance to it—why not [assistance] from the Himalayas, the Vindhya mountains, and so forth as well?

If it is argued that "this belongs to that" because of a relation between them, then what is the relation between the beneficiary and the benefactor? It cannot be conjunction (*saṃyoga*), since that exists only between two substances; however, in this case, the beneficiary is a substance while the benefit is an action, so there is no conjunction. Nor can it be inherence (*samavāya*), because since inherence is unitary and all-pervading, it is equal everywhere due to the absence of proximity or distance; thus, it is not logical for it to be related only to specific relata. And if a relation with specific relata were admitted...

An assistance rendered by that [cause] must be admitted for this inherence; and such being the case, the conceptualization of the difference or non-difference of that assistance remains in the same state [of difficulty].

If there were non-difference [of the entity] from its causal efficacy due to inherence (*samavāya*), then inherence itself would be what is produced. On the other hand, if there is difference, then even for inherence, there can be no status as a relation unless it has a fixed connection. Therefore, an entity that is absolutely eternal performs purposeful action neither successively nor simultaneously. For it is not perceived that a single entity performs all actions occurring at all times simultaneously. Or, even if it did so, what would it do in the second moment? If it were to act then, the fault inherent in the position of succession would follow.

However, if [the entity] were not to act, it would follow that it lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) and thus would be a non-entity. Therefore, causal efficiency—which is pervaded by both succession and simultaneity—is excluded when its pervader is absent, by virtue of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Consequently, being excluded, causal efficiency excludes its own pervaded property, existence (*sattva*). Thus, the position of absolute permanence cannot withstand logical scrutiny.

The position that [everything] is exclusively impermanent is also not worthy of acceptance; for that which is impermanent perishes at every moment, and such a thing is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through succession, because there is an absence of both spatial and temporal succession. For succession is priority and posteriority, and that is impossible for a momentary entity. Indeed, it is only for a persisting thing that pervasion across various places and times is designated as spatial succession and temporal succession; and this [pervasion] does not exist in that which is subject to destruction. As they say: "Whatever is in whatever place is in that very place; whatever is at whatever time is at that very time. There is no pervasion of entities across space and time here."

Furthermore, a sequence of preceding and succeeding moments cannot exist in dependence upon a continuum (*santāna*), because the continuum is not a real entity (*avastu*). Even if it were a real entity, if it were momentary, it would have no distinction from the moments themselves; if, on the other hand, it were non-momentary, then the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) would be utterly destroyed. Nor is causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) possible for a momentary thing through a non-sequential process. For that single moment of a citron’s form and so forth, in producing multiple subsequent moments of taste and so forth simultaneously, would have to produce them either by means of a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or by means of multiple intrinsic natures.

If it acts by means of a single [nature], then those moments of taste and so forth would be one, because they would not differ from the single nature of the tasting. Now, if it produces some things, such as form and so forth, through its diverse natures by way of being their material cause (*upādāna*), and other things, such as taste and so forth, by way of being their cooperative condition (*sahakārin*), then are those natures identical with its essence (*ātmabhūta*) or not identical with its essence? If they are not identical with its essence, then its status as a "nature" is lost. If they are identical with its essence, then it must be manifold because it possesses multiple natures; or else, the natures themselves would have to be one, because they are not distinct from it and it is one.

If it is claimed that the very same thing which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) in one instance serves as the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) in another, and thus no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) is admitted; then how can a proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) admit both a difference in intrinsic nature and a confusion of effects for an eternal entity that is uniform in nature yet produces diverse effects sequentially?

Now, if it is argued that because the eternal is of a single nature, it is devoid of succession (*akrama*), and how then can there be the production of successive, diverse effects from that which lacks succession? Ah, what a partisan of his own position the "Beloved of the Gods" (the opponent) is! For while he himself accepts that multiple effects—each to be accomplished by multiple causes—arise simultaneously from a single, partless cause characterized as a momentary form (*rūpa*) and so forth, he nevertheless raises an objection regarding the opposing view: that even for an eternal entity, there is a contradiction in its producing diverse effects sequentially. Therefore, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) occurs even for a momentary entity without succession.

Since "difficult to establish" means that even from the absolute standpoint of impermanence, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—which is pervaded by both succession and simultaneity—is excluded precisely through their negation; and since, upon its exclusion, existence (*sattva*) itself is also negated by the force of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), the doctrine of absolute impermanence is not tenable. In the *syādvāda*, however, the performance of causal efficiency by entities is not contradictory, as it occurs through transformation (*pariṇāma*) characterized by the relinquishing of a prior form, the assuming of a subsequent form, and the persistence [of the substance].

Nor should it be said that the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness) is untenable because of the imposition of mutually contradictory properties upon a single entity; for a distinct alternative position—one that is neither exclusively eternal nor exclusively non-eternal, but consists of both existence and non-existence in some respect—is accepted, and it is precisely as such that it is affirmed by all. Thus they recite: "That object which is a lion in one part and a man in another part, consisting of two parts yet being partless, is designated as Narasiṃha (the Man-Lion) through its divisions."

By this [argument], he refutes the absolute universal, the absolute particular, and the view that the universal and the particular are distinct; for instance: are particulars different from the universal or not? If they are different, they would be like the mass of hair on a frog's head [i.e., utterly insignificant]; if they are not different, then they are identical to it, just as its own nature is—thus there is the absolute universal. Those who maintain the absolute universal include the various Mīmāṃsakas who follow the *dravyāstika-naya* (substantialist perspective), the Advaitins, and the Sāṃkhyas.

Those who follow the method of the "modes" (paryāyanaya) declare that only the distinct, momentary particulars are the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because a universal (*sāmānya*) existing as something separate from them is not perceived. Indeed, at the time when one perceives individuals such as cows and the like, nothing else whatsoever—apart from the specific form of the individual consisting of color and shape—that is unitary and pervasive, appears in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for there is no such experience. And thus they recite: "While these five fingers are clearly manifesting in perceptual cognition..."
He who perceives the common form beholds the horn upon his own head.

However, since the cognition that apprehends a single form arises from the individuals themselves—possessing powers imparted by their own causes—it is not logical to use that [cognition] as a proof for a universal.

Furthermore, this universal (*sāmānya*) that is postulated—whether it be one or many, and if one, whether all-pervading (*sarvagata*) or not all-pervading—if it were all-pervading, why is it not perceived even in the intervals between individual instances? Or, if its all-pervasive oneness is admitted, then just as the universal "cowness" encompasses individual cows, why does it not likewise encompass individuals such as jars and cloths, since there is no distinction [between them]? If, on the other hand, it were not all-pervading, it would follow that it assumes a specific form (*viśeṣarūpa*), which contradicts its own definition.

Now, [if it is argued that] the universal is manifold because it is differentiated by distinctions such as "cowness," "horseness," and "potness," then it follows that only particulars (*viśeṣa*) are accepted, since they are the causes for mutual exclusion; for that which is "cowness" is not identical in nature to "horseness. Furthermore, the definition of a real entity (*vastu*) is its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and this is clearly observed only in particulars. No causal efficiency whatsoever is performed by a universal, because it is devoid of action; for in causal activities such as carrying or milking, only particulars are of use. Thus, this universal [is distinct] from the particulars.

Is it different or non-different? If it is different, it is a non-entity, because it lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyā) due to its separation from the particular (viśeṣa). If it is non-different, then the particulars themselves are its very nature; thus, there is the doctrine of the absolute reality of the particular (viśeṣaikāntavāda).

But those who follow the *naigama-naya* say: "The universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are independent, because they are perceived as such by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, the universal and the particular are absolutely distinct, because they are characterized by contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharma-adhyāsita*); whatever is so is so, just like water and fire; and these two are so; therefore, they are so. Indeed, the universal, such as 'cowness' (*gotva*), is all-pervading (*sarvagata*), whereas the particulars, such as the brindled cow and the black-spotted cow, are the opposite of that. Therefore, how could their identity be logical? [The particular] is not separate from the universal."
If it is argued that there is the perception of a particularity, then how is that perception to be explained? It must be stated.

If it is argued that [the object] is pervaded by the universal (*sāmānya*), we say no; for in that case, there would be no apprehension of the particular (*viśeṣa*), since the universal alone would be grasped by that cognition. Consequently, because that cognition lacks the apprehension of a distinct particular, the cognizer would not employ the word expressive of it nor engage in the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) accomplished by it. Yet this is not the case, as we observe the employment of both the naming and the usage of particulars. Therefore, one who desires to express a particular and intends to engage in its usage must admit a cognition that apprehends that particular.

Thus, by employing the word for the particular (*viśeṣa*) in the place of the universal (*sāmānya*), and the word for the universal in the place of the particular, one must admit that even regarding the universal, there is a distinct cognition that apprehends it. Therefore, because both appear separately in the cognition that grasps each of them, the two are mutually disjointed; consequently, it is not possible for an entity to consist of both universal and particular. This is the doctrine of independent universals and particulars (*svatantra-sāmānya-viśeṣa-vāda*). The followers of Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda are proponents of this doctrine of independent universals and particulars, in accordance with the *naigama-naya*.

All three of these positions cannot withstand scrutiny, as they are contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For an entity consisting of both the universal and the particular is experienced without dispute; indeed, the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of a real thing is its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and investigators maintain that this is fully accounted for only within the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*).

For instance, when the word "cow" is uttered, there is the cognition of an entity possessing parts such as hooves, humps, tails, dewlaps, and horns, which conforms to all individual instances; at that time, the exclusion of buffaloes and the like is also cognized. Even where it is said, "a brindled cow," just as there is the manifestation of a particular [quality], the manifestation of "cowness" (*gotva*) is likewise perfectly clear. Even when only the particular is uttered as "brindled," "cowness" follows by implication or from the context.

Moreover, variegation (*śabala*) is also manifold in form, as is observed in experience. Therefore, when a speaker says "variegated," the variegation intended—which is inherent in the specific cow being referred to—is established as encompassing the universal of variegation. Thus, even though the nature of things as consisting of both the universal and the particular is well-known and recognized by everyone from children to cowherds, the doctrine of absolute exclusivity regarding either one is mere prattle. For nowhere, at no time, and by no one is any universal ever experienced devoid of particulars, nor are particulars ever experienced devoid of that [universal]. As they have said: [The verse follows: "Even in the case of a single object, such as a cow, there is a difference between its various states; how much more so in the case of objects that are diverse? etc.
"Where, when, by whom, and in what form have substance separated from its modes, or modes devoid of substance, ever been perceived by any means of valid cognition? Thus [it is said].
Only those of poor intellect, due to the intense delusion produced by the power of fallacious reasoning, deny one [aspect] and establish another; this is the "blind men and the elephant" analogy.

Furthermore, even those faults previously mentioned that assail the position of absolute monism (ekāntapakṣa) are not capable of even breathing, having been shattered by the fierce blows of the mallet of the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda).

However, those who maintain that universals and particulars are independent entities must be refuted as follows: A universal is in some sense distinct from each individual, and in some sense identical with it, because it consists of dissimilar modifications (*visadṛśapariṇāma*). For just as a certain individual, when perceived, is established as distinct from another individual due to the observation of dissimilar modifications, so too is it established as "similar" due to the observation of a universal consisting of similar modifications. This is because of the cognition: "This cow is similar to that," or "That is similar to this."

Nor does its nature as a universal (sāmānya) suffer contradiction because it is non-different from the individual's own form (*vyakti-svarūpa*), since even color and other qualities (*rūpādi*) are non-different from the individual's own form, yet their status as qualities (*guṇa-rūpatā*) is not contradicted. Furthermore, there is indeed some degree of distinction (*kathañcid-vyatireka*) between the universal and the similar modification (*sadṛśa-pariṇāma*), just as there is between color and so forth, because the latter possesses separate designations and the like. Moreover, particularities (*viśeṣas*) cannot be entirely distinct from the universal; for if the universal were established as being omnipresent (*sarvagata*), then those [particularities] would be non-omnipresent, which would result in the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharmādhyāsa*).

And that [oneness] is not established for it, because it has been refuted by the reasoning stated previously; for since the universal and the particulars are established as having both a single and multiple nature through their being in some way non-different from one another, the universal is held to be multiple because it is non-different from the particulars, and the particulars are also of a single form because they are non-different from the universal. Thus, oneness of the universal is to be understood everywhere from the perspective of the *saṃgraha-naya*, while its multiplicity is to be understood from the perspective of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that which consists of a similar modification differs with each individual instance, just like dissimilar modifications.

Thus, the claim that the universal and the particular are in every respect possessed of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsitatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). If, however, what is intended is that they are possessed of contradictory attributes in some respect (*kathañcit*), then you have entered our own position; for being possessed of contradictory attributes in some respect is invariably concomitant with being distinct in some respect (*kathañcidbheda*). Furthermore, the example of water and fire is devoid of both the probandum and the probans, because even those two are accepted as being distinct and as being possessed of contradictory attributes in some respect, by virtue of [their respective] properties such as liquidity (*payastva*) and fiery heat (*pāvakatva*).

There is a superimposition of contradictory properties and a distinction between those two, yet by way of their substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, there is the opposite of that; thus, how could it not be the case that a real entity possesses the nature of both universal and particular? And it has been said: "Even though the treatise was composed by Ulūka (Vaiśeṣika) through these two [categories], it is nevertheless false, because its own objects are mutually independent due to their distinct natures."

"Even though the treatise was composed by Ulūka according to both systems, it is nevertheless false, because [the two systems] are mutually independent due to their respective predominance over their own objects.
Likewise: "For a universal without particularity would be like the horn of a donkey."
For particulars are likewise devoid of universals.

Likewise, absolute existence and absolute non-existence are indeed untenable; for such is the case: the very nature of all entities consists in being both existent and non-existent. If an entity were absolutely existent, it would lack its own specific character (*vaisvarūpya*); and if it were absolutely non-existent, entities would be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Therefore, because it exists by way of its own form and does not exist by way of another’s form, an entity is established as being of the nature of both existence and non-existence. As they have said: "Everything exists by way of its own form and does not exist by way of another’s form;
otherwise, there would be the existence of everything [indiscriminately], or else even the existence of its own form would be impossible."

Consequently, since all objects other than the jar exist within a single jar in the form of its absence (*abhāva*), it is easily established that the jar possesses a manifold nature (*anekāntātmakatva*). And thus, when one object is known, all objects are known; for without the determination of all things, it is impossible to determine a single entity in its distinctness as consisting of the negation of those [others]. Scripture also establishes this very point: "He who knows the One knows all;
he who knows all knows the One."
(He who knows one, knows all;
he who knows all, knows one.
Likewise: "By whom one entity is seen in every way, by him all entities are seen in every way."
By whom all things have been seen in every way, by him one thing has been seen in every way.

Thus, a thing is easily established as having the nature of non-absolutism consisting of both existence and non-existence; by this very method, it should also be understood that because the expansion of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*)—beginning with "in some sense it exists," "in some sense it does not exist," and "in some sense it is inexpressible"—pervades the multitude of all worldly categories, it consists of both the expressible and the inexpressible.

[The Lord] is the teacher of the reality of things as they truly are; having brought about the destruction of all karma—that is, having effected the exhaustion and shedding (*nirjarana*) of all karmas, both those that destroy and those that do not destroy, which are the material particles (*pudgala*) to be experienced by the soul—he attained the supreme state.

For others, such as the followers of Sugata and other traditions, even after attaining liberation, descend again and again into cyclic existence whenever there is an occasion for the humiliation of their religious order (tīrtha) and so forth. As they say: "The knowers, who are the founders of the ford of Dharma, having gone to the supreme state, return once more to existence due to the humiliation of their religious order."

In the ultimate sense, they do not possess the state of liberation because of the absence of the destruction of karma; for when karma is truly destroyed, there is no further entry into rebirth. As it has been said: "Just as a sprout does not emerge at all once the seed is burnt, so too, when the seed of karma is burnt, the sprout of existence does not grow."
And the Blessed One, being an Arhat, attained the state of Śiva even prior to the exhaustion of his karma. || 45-46 ||

In their doctrine, there are nine principles (tattvas): the soul (jīva) and the non-soul (ajīva), as well as merit (puṇya), demerit (pāpa), influx (āsrava), restraint (saṃvara), bondage (bandha), dissociation (nirjarā), and liberation (mokṣa).
He states the principles (*tattva*) with the words "jīva and ajīva," and so forth.
It should be understood that, according to that system—the Jaina system—nine principles exist; their names are established by the literal reading itself. (47)
[In a pair:
Therein, [the self] is distinct from yet non-different from qualities such as knowledge;
it is the agent of auspicious and inauspicious actions, and the enjoyer of the fruit of those actions. (48)

The soul (jīva) is characterized by consciousness, while that which possesses the opposite qualities is declared to be non-soul (ajīva). Merit (puṇya) consists of the material particles (pudgala) of virtuous action.
He explains the principles of *jīva* (the soul) and *ajīva* (the non-soul), beginning with the words "In that [system]," and so forth.

In that Jaina doctrine, the connection is that the *jīva* is characterized by consciousness (*caitanya*). He states its qualifications: "distinct and non-distinct from attributes such as knowledge. This means that this *jīva*, although possessing fourteen types of divisions, is in some sense distinct and in some sense non-distinct from those attributes—knowledge, perception, conduct, and so on—which constitute the qualities of the soul. These are the attributes whose first is knowledge; thus, the meaning is that the *jīva* is both different and not different from these qualities of knowledge, perception, and conduct.

From one-sensed beings up to those with five senses, there is indeed possession of knowledge from their own perspective; thus, there is non-difference [of the soul] from knowledge and so forth. However, from the perspective of another, there is a lack of knowledge, which constitutes difference. If even slightly there were no possession of knowledge in all living beings, then the living being would attain the state of a non-living being. And thus says the established doctrine (siddhānta):
"Of all living beings, an infinite fraction of the syllable [of consciousness] is eternally uncovered."
If that [karma] were also insentient, then the soul would attain the state of being non-sentient;
for even though the light of the moon and sun is pure, it becomes obscured by the gathering of clouds.
An infinite portion of the imperishable life-force of all living beings is eternally uncovered;
if even that were covered, then the living being would become a non-living thing.
Even the pure light of the moon and sun becomes obscured by the gathering of clouds.

Likewise, [the term] "possessing transformation" (*vivṛttimān*): *vivṛtti* means transformation (*pariṇāma*). The suffix *-mat* indicates that this [soul] possesses it; the meaning is that the soul experiences various forms of transformation consisting of births among the classes of gods, humans, hell-beings, and animals, ranging from those with one sense-organ up to those with five.

Furthermore, there is the agent who performs auspicious and inauspicious karma; the auspicious is that which is to be experienced as pleasant (*sātavedya*), and the inauspicious is that which is to be experienced as unpleasant (*asātavedya*). "Auspicious and inauspicious" is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). Such karma—which constitutes the object to be experienced—is "the agent," meaning the one who establishes it within his own self, or in other words, the one who acquires it. And unlike the Sāṅkhya view, the self is not a non-agent who is unbound by good or evil; likewise, he is not merely an agent, but also an experiencer—the one who feels the fruit of the merit and demerit acquired by himself, for one person does not experience what was done by another. Thus says the scripture: [The original Sanskrit text follows this: *anyacca śubhāśubhaṃ karma karttā, śubhaṃ sātavedyamaṣ aśubhamasātavedyaṃ, śubhañcāśubhañceti dvandvaḥ, evaṃvidhaṃ karma bhoktavyalakarttṛbhūtaṃ karttā svātmasādvidhātā upārjayiteti yāvad, na ca sāṅkhyavadakartā''tmā śubhāśubhābandhakaśceti tathā karmaphalambhoktā na ca kevalaḥ karttā, kiṃ tu bhoktā'pi svopārjitapuṇyapāpakarmaphalasya vedayitā na cānyakṛtasyānyo bhoktā| tathā cāgamaḥ —* (Note: The provided source text contains a repetition of the initial portion of the commentary. The translation above reflects the full logical structure of the argument as presented.)
"Venerable Sir, for living beings, is suffering self-made, is suffering made by another, or is suffering made by both?
"Gautama, suffering is self-made."
Suffering is not made by another, nor is suffering made by both. Thus it is said.
"Venerable sir, is suffering for living beings self-made, is suffering made by another, or is suffering made by both?
Gotama, suffering is not self-made, nor is suffering made by another, nor is suffering made by both."

"Like the agent, so too is the enjoyer, characterized by consciousness (*caitanya*). Consciousness is the nature of sentience; that which has this as its characteristic—that is, its fundamental attribute—is [the soul]. Thus, all fourteen varieties of living beings—including those divided into subtle and gross, those with one sense organ, those with three deficient senses, and those with five sense organs divided into the conscious (*saṃjñin*) and the unconscious (*asaṃjñin*), as well as those who are fully developed (*paryāpta*) and those who are not—do not deviate from consciousness.

Now he speaks of the non-soul (*ajīva*): "And that which possesses the opposite of this is declared to be the non-soul. Furthermore, that which possesses the opposite—that is, a state of being otherwise—than those characteristics of the soul, having a contrary nature and being insentient (*acetana*), is declared and described by the former sages as the non-soul. Its subdivisions are: merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), space (*ākāśa*), matter (*pudgala*), aggregates (*skandha*), partial aggregates (*deśa*), ultimate particles (*pradeśa*), qualities (*guṇa*), time (*addhā*), the absolute (*kevala*), and the atom (*paramāṇu*). These constitute the fourth category, the subdivisions of the non-soul.

"Merit consists of the *pudgalas* of wholesome karma. To the question "What is the nature of that reality called merit?", he says: "The *pudgalas* of wholesome karma. "Wholesome" (*sat*) means beautiful or pleasant-to-be-experienced (*sātavedya*); "its *pudgalas*" refers to the particles that constitute its portions, meaning the meritorious types of matter (*prakṛtis*). These are forty-two, as follows: Human, subhuman, celestial, and long life; Pleasant-feeling, obstructive, and bodily luster; Tirthankara, high status, beautiful formation, Five-sensed, mobile, and symmetrical body.

Human, subhuman, and celestial lifespans; high status; pleasant feeling; harming others, fame, and radiance; the non-heavy-light [touch]; and the first mode of movement—these forty-two are the auspicious types of karma.
The underlying meaning is not stated here for fear of excessive length of the text; such is the sense of the verse. (48–49)
That which is the opposite of merit is evil, and false belief and so forth are its causes;
that bondage produced by them is to be known as *āsrava* (influx) in the teaching of the Jina. (50)
He states the remaining category [of karma] with the words beginning "pāpam" (evil):

"But again, that which is the opposite of that, dissimilar to the nature of merit (puṇya-prakṛti), is evil (pāpa); this is the meaning of the category of evil. And "mithyātvādyāḥ" (falsehood and so forth): falsehood (mithyā-darśana), non-abstinence (avirati), negligence (pramāda), passions (kaṣāya), and activity (yoga) are the causes, the reasons for evil; and its types (tat-prakṛtayaḥ) are eighty-two, as follows: the ten immobile [karmas], the four births, the non-primary figures, movements, skeletons, and structures.
The fourfold group of hellish states, the two types of infernal births, the fourfold group of colors, and the forty names.
Nārāyaṇīya, Āśāta-ghāti, Pañcacatvāriṃśat-sahasra-vārṣika. Thus [ends the section].
The ten stationary [karmas], the four types of birth, the non-primary figures, the movement of birds, and the nine [types of] formation.
The two [types of] lifespan in the animal and hell realms, the four [categories of] birth, and the four colors—these constitute forty names.
When combined with the lifespan in the hells, the low status, and the five [types of] murderers, they total eighty-two.

There are eighty-two sinful dispositions (pāpaprakṛtis) distinct from the meritorious ones. However, there is no fault regarding the four castes (varṇas), as they are connected to both [merit and demerit] by way of being both auspicious and inauspicious. That bondage of karma which is caused by those [factors] such as false view (mithyādarśana) and so forth is to be understood as "influx" (āśrava) in the teaching of the Jina; the meaning is that the reality of influx (āśravatattva) is to be known. Its specific types (prakṛtis) are forty-two, as follows: the five senses, the four passions (kaṣāyas), the five vows (vratas), mind, speech, and body, and the twenty-five activities (kriyās) beginning with bodily activity (kāyikī); such is influx. (50)
Restraint is the cessation of that [influx]; however, bondage is the soul's connection with karma.
This bond between the two arises from their mutual interpenetration. (51)

Furthermore, its cessation is the obstruction of the gates of the *āsravas*; it is the reality of restraint (*saṃvara*). As for the constituent elements of restraint, they are fifty-seven, as follows: the five *samitis*, the three *guptis*, the twenty-two *parīṣahas*, the ten *yati-dharmas*, the twelve *bhāvanās*, and the five types of conduct (*cāritra*). Thus, [the total] is fifty-seven.
The vows, restraints, hardships, duties of an ascetic, meditations,
and conducts consist of fifty types, categorized as five, three, twenty-two, ten, twelve, and five respectively.

The five *samitis*, the three *guptis*, the twenty-two *parīṣahas*, the tenfold *yatidharma*, the twelve *bhāvanās*, and the five *cāritras* constitute the [eighteen] *prakṛtis*. As for "bondage" (*bandha*): it refers to the connection or conjunction between the living soul (*jīva*)—the sentient being—and the karma that is to be experienced, resulting from their mutual interpenetration according to the analogy of milk and water becoming blended. This is the meaning of the principle called bondage. It is fourfold, distinguished by *prakṛti*, *sthiti*, *anubhāga*, and *pradeśa*: "Intrinsic nature is declared to be *prakṛti*; *sthiti* is the determination of duration."
The "anubhāga" (potency) is to be known as the "rasa" (taste), and the "pradeśa" (spatial extent) is the accumulation of "dala" (leaves/particles).
Such is the relationship to be understood. || 51 ||
The shedding of bound karma is considered *nirjarā* (dissociation);
however, the absolute separation from the body and so forth is called *mokṣa* (liberation). || 52 ||
He explains *nirjarā* (dissociation) and *mokṣa* (liberation) with the words beginning "of that which is bound" (*baddhasya*).

Furthermore, *nirjarā* is considered by the ancient masters to be the shedding (*śāṭa*) or destruction of karma—that karma which has been acquired in the forms of *sṛṣṭa*, *baddha*, *nidhatta*, *nikācita*, and so forth—through the practice of austerity, meditation, recitation, and the like. This, moreover, is twofold, distinguished as *sakāma* (with desire) and *akāma* (without desire). Furthermore, *mokṣa* is said to be the absolute separation from the body and other such things. And it is ninefold, as follows: [1] *saṃtāpa* (heat), [2] *varūvaṇayā* (expiation), [3] *davva* (substance), [4] *māṇa* (measure), [5] *khitta* (space), [6] *pasaṇā* (time)... [text continues].
Time, interval, part, state, and indeed the few and the many—thus [it is said].
(The exposition of the six states, the measure of substance, the spatial field, contact, time, interval, division, mode, and relative abundance.
Indeed, there are nine types [of liberation]; "liberation" (*śiva*) means the absolute non-existence of external vital breaths due to their never returning again.

If it is argued that there would be the undesirable consequence of being lifeless (*ajīvatva*) due to the total absence of *prāṇas*, and consequently, because of being included within the second category of reality (*tattva*), there would be an absence of the principle of liberation (*mokṣatattva*); [we reply: no. For in liberation, there is indeed the absence of only the *dravya-prāṇas* (substantial vitalities), whereas the *bhāva-prāṇas* (functional vitalities) exist even in the state of desirelessness (*naiṣkāmika*). As it has been said:

"Because [the soul in liberation] is endowed with absolute right conviction (*kṣāyika-samyaktva*), as well as with absolute energy, perfection, vision, and knowledge, and also with a happiness free from dualities."
"Knowledge and the other [virtues], however, are the life-force of existence; therefore, even when liberated, one continues to live.
Consequently, the state of being alive is indeed eternal for every living being."

The meaning of the verse is that liberation arises from the separation of the soul from the body it has joined; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the absence of connection with the body, the senses, and their attributes is also included. || 52 ||
He who, with a firm disposition, has faith in these principles therein, possesses the fitness for right conduct through the application of right knowledge. (53)
Having thus proclaimed the principles (tattvas) by mentioning their names, he states the conclusion preceded by the result, beginning with "etāni tatra" and so forth.

These aforementioned principles, in that system of the Jina, whoever—being of stable disposition and firm mind—has faith in them, meaning they considers them without error; for one who, despite knowing them, lacks faith, is merely a person of false view.

As it has been said in the *Śrī-Gandhi-hasti-mahātarka*: "Even the twelvefold scripture (*dvādaśāṅga-śruta*) is false for one who lacks right vision. For such a person of firm mind, there is fitness for conduct (*cāritra-yogyatā*) through the union with rightness (*samyaktva-yoga*), and worthiness for conduct (*cāritrārhatā*) through the union of rightness and knowledge (*samyaktva-jñāna-yoga*). Rightness and knowledge are "rightness-knowledge" (*samyaktva-jñāne*); the mention of these two is for the purpose of excluding that conduct which is devoid of knowledge and vision—that is, to distinguish it from what is not right conduct (*samyak-cāritra*). || 53 ||

Likewise, for one in whom these three [factors] have matured through the ripening of their spiritual capacity (bhavyatva), they become a vessel for liberation through the union of right knowledge and action. || 54 ||

He states the result with the words beginning "by the ripening of fitness" (*bhavyatvapākena*). The word "thus" (*tathā*) is used for illustration. By the ripening of fitness—that is, by the state of fitness having reached full maturity—liberation must necessarily be attained in that very life. Through the ripening of such fitness, if this triad consisting of right vision, knowledge, and conduct should arise in a person, then—since there is an inherent connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*—that person is understood even though not explicitly mentioned; the meaning is that he becomes a vessel for liberation and enjoys the glory of *nirvāṇa*. Why? Because of the union of right knowledge and action. Regarding the word "right" (*samyak*): [it means]...

Rightness (*samyaktva*) is vision (*darśana*); knowledge (*jñāna*) is the comprehension of the scriptures; and conduct (*kriyā*) consists of the *caraṇa* and *karaṇa* [observances]. From the conjunction—that is, the connection—of these [three], and not from vision, knowledge, or conduct alone, does liberation arise. As the venerable Bhadrabāhusvāmin said:
"Of what use is even a vast amount of heard scripture to one devoid of conduct?
It is like millions of billions of lamps set ablaze for a blind man."
"What will even a vast amount of learning and study avail one who is devoid of conduct?
It is like a lamp for a blind man, even if it be hundreds of thousands of millions of lamps.
Likewise: "Knowledge devoid of conduct, and the assumption of the [monastic] insignia devoid of right view..."
And for him who practices austerity devoid of self-restraint, it is meaningless.
"Knowledge devoid of conduct, the assumption of emblems devoid of right vision, and austerity devoid of self-restraint—all these are useless for him.

Indeed, it is only when right vision, knowledge, and conduct are combined that they become the causes of liberation, as the Chief of Expositors [Umāsvāti] stated: "Right vision, knowledge, and conduct constitute the path to liberation. (54)
Perception and inference are thus considered the two means of valid cognition;
for in this system, an object possessing infinite properties is the domain of these means of cognition.

Regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "Perception," and so forth. The word "thus" (*tathā*) refers to the connection with the subject matter under discussion; two means of valid cognition are accepted—that is, intended. He asks which they are and says: "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) and "indirect" (*parokṣa*). *Akṣa* is that which pervades (*aśnute*) or extends over (*akṣṇoti*) all substances, places, times, and states; thus, *akṣa* refers to the soul (*jīva*), and *akṣa* also refers to the sense organ (*indriya*), as it perceives its object. "Perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is that knowledge which has gone toward each respective sense organ (*akṣaṃ akṣaṃ prati gataṃ*); the meaning is that it is the knowledge arising by depending upon the sense organs which establishes empirical usage.

The knowledge of limited range (*avadhi*), mind-reading (*manaḥparyāya*), and omniscience (*kevalajñāna*), along with their subdivisions, are indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For this very reason, the various classifications such as conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*), ultimate (*pāramārthika*), sensory (*aindriyika*), and supersensory (*atīndriyika*) are included within these alone, because they manifest specific types of knowledge that exceed [the scope of] inference (*anumāna*). And there is "indirect" (*parokṣa*). It is called indirect because it is beyond the senses (*akṣa*), or because it exists apart from the senses, or because it is perceived by something other than the senses, such as memory. Indirect knowledge has the subdivisions of recollection (*smaraṇa*), recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), reasoning (*tarka*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*). By this same method, the two types of knowledge—sensory cognition (*mati*) and verbal testimony (*śruta*)—are also exclusively indirect; thus, there are two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Having stated the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he states its object (*gocara*): "Furthermore (*tu punaḥ*), here in the Jina’s doctrine, the object of the means of valid cognition—the scope (*gocara*) of the two means of valid cognition, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*parokṣa*)—is to be known. To the question "What is that?", [the answer is] "an entity (*vastu*) possessing infinite attributes (*anantadharmaka*). What is the specific characteristic of the reality of the entity (*vastutattva*), the nature of the thing (*padārthasvarūpa*)? It is "possessing infinite attributes," meaning that which has infinite—that is, immeasurable—attributes (*dharma*), both coexistent and successively occurring *paryāyas*, because they have the three times as their domain. By this, the proof (*sādhana*) is also shown; for instance: "existence" (*sattva*) is the property-bearer (*dharmin*).

The property to be proven (*sādhya*) is the state of having infinite properties as its essence; "because existence would otherwise be impossible" is the reason (*hetu*). Since the reason has the single characteristic of being impossible otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), the probandum is established by internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) alone, and thus there is no need for examples and so forth. This is a purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) reason, because positive examples (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*)—such as "whatever does not have infinite properties as its essence is not existent, like a sky-lotus"—are included within the scope of the subject (*pakṣa*) and thus cannot function as a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
