Regarding the self (*ātman*), its nature as consisting of infinite attributes includes co-existent (*sahabhāvin*) qualities such as the capacity for both cognitive application with form (*sākāra-upayoga*) and without form (*anākāra-upayoga*), agency (*kartṛtva*), enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*), immobility within eight spatial points (*pradeśa*), incorporeality (*amūrtatva*), the state of possessing innumerable spatial points (*asaṅkhyāta-pradeśātmakatā*), and the quality of being a living soul (*jīvatva*). On the other hand, qualities such as joy, dejection, grief, pleasure, pain, and the states of being a god, a hell-being, an animal, or a human are successive (*kramabhāvin*). Similarly, among the categories of existence such as the medium of motion (*dharmāstikāya*), there are attributes such as the state of possessing innumerable spatial points, the capacity to facilitate movement and so forth, and the state of being an object of knowledge through cognition such as sensory perception (*mati-jñāna*).

[The qualities of] being delimited by this or that specific delimiter, having a fixed state, being formless, possessing a single substance, and being inactive, and so forth; whereas in the case of a jar, there are [qualities such as] being unbaked, possessing color and other qualities produced by baking, having a broad base, a belly, and a conch-like neck, the capacity for holding and carrying water and other liquids, being the object of cognitions such as memory, being new, and being old, and so forth.

Thus, regarding all categories of objects, one who is proficient in the various systems and doctrines should understand, based on both verbal and non-verbal synonyms, that even within the words used to express them, there exist distinctions such as acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), open (*vivṛta*), closed (*saṃvṛta*), voiced (*ghoṣavat*), unvoiced (*aghoṣa*), aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*), and unaspirated (*alpaprāṇa*), as well as the respective capacities for conveying specific meanings. Because of this reason, the power [of opposing arguments] is shattered by the blow of the fierce hammer of non-absolutism (*anekānta*); thus, there is no room at all for logical thorns such as the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), or the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). The meaning is that such a reality, which is exceedingly beautiful through its manifold synonyms, is the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the Jina’s teaching. || 55 ||

Such knowledge that apprehends an object through direct perception is called *pratyakṣa* (perception); other [knowledge] is to be known as *parokṣa* (indirect), with respect to its mode of apprehension. 56.
Having stated the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), he states the definition (*lakṣaṇa*): "by way of immediacy" (*aparokṣatayā*).

In this context, "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is the statement of the object to be defined; "a cognition that apprehends an object by way of immediacy"—such is the statement of the definition. "Mediate" (*parokṣa*) means beyond the range of the senses; that which is other than this is "immediate" (*aparokṣa*). Its state is "immediacy" (*tattā*), meaning by way of being directly perceived (*sākṣātkṛtatayā*). "Object" (*artha*) means that which is sought after (*arthyate*), the sense being that it is understood (*gamyate*); or alternatively, "object" (*artha*) refers to purposeful action such as burning or cooking, which is desired (*abhilaṣyate*) by those seeking it. A "cognition" (*jñāna*) is that which apprehends it—that is, that which determines it through a definitive ascertainment (*vyavasāyātmakatayā*).

"It is of such a kind" (*tadīdṛśam*); the connection is that "it is precisely of such a kind as direct perception" (*pratyakṣam*). By the term "by way of being non-indirect" (*aparokṣatayā*), he excludes from direct perception any confusion with the definition of indirect [perception], because the latter consists in grasping an object through a lack of immediate presence. Regarding the phrase "of such a kind": by this, however, through the previously stated reasoning and by demonstrating a cognition characterized by a collection of qualifiers with an exclusive emphasis (*sāvadhāraṇatvena*), he rejects the status of direct perception for the "reasoning" (*yukti*) postulated by others.

Thus, when they say: "Perception is knowledge arising from the contact of the sense organs with their objects, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature," as well as: "When there is a correct conjunction of a person's sense organs, the birth of cognition is perception," and so forth—that is shown to be incorrect. This is because the manifestation of something previously non-existent is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and because it would entail the absurd consequence that even utterly non-existent things, such as a rabbit's horn, could arise. Therefore, this [perception] exists only as the very nature of the Self.

It is produced through the presence of a collection of causes that effect its specific qualities, in the form of a transformation consisting of the direct apprehension of an object; thus, the qualification "having arisen" with respect to form and so forth would not be possible. If you were to say that this [text] merely indicates such an object, then let it be that it is simply non-cognition (avijñāna); for now, let that suffice.

Now he demonstrates the definition of indirect cognition (*parokṣa-lakṣaṇa*) with the words "the other," and so forth. Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has been defined as the cognition that grasps an object through immediacy; therefore, the cognition that grasps an object non-directly should be known and understood as indirect (*parokṣa*). Yet, showing that this too is indeed direct with respect to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), but receives the designation "indirect" with respect to external objects, he says: "with regard to the act of grasping."

In this context, "grasping" (grahaṇa) refers to the external operation [of the senses] due to the context; otherwise, the qualification would be redundant. Its "expectation" (īkṣā)—that is, its dependence on the extensive consideration of the operation—is what is meant. Thus, the meaning is as follows: although [the cognition] itself is direct perception, it is nevertheless called "indirect" (parokṣa) because it functions through the mediation of signs (liṅga), words (śabda), and so forth, in the grasping of external objects, by way of being non-immediate (asākṣātkāritayā). This is the sense. || 56 ||
That which is endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence is held to be existent;
therefore, a thing possessing infinite properties is said to be the domain of valid cognition. (57)

Reaffirming the very reality of things already mentioned by way of its nature as consisting of infinite attributes (*anantadharmātmaka*), he says: "By which [there is] arising," and so forth. For whatever reason—that which is endowed with arising (*utpāda*), passing away (*vyaya*), and persistence (*dhrauvya*) is accepted as being existent (*sat*) and having the nature of existence (*sattvarūpa*)—for that reason, the entity (*vastu*) possessing infinite attributes is the domain of valid cognition (*māna*), meaning it is the object of both direct (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect (*parokṣa*) means of knowledge; this is the connection to the statement "it has been said" (*uktam*). Arising, passing away, and persistence are "arising-passing-away-persistence"; the knowledge that their combination is itself existence (*sattva*) is the intended meaning.

It is "sought" (iṣyate) in the sense that it is desired by those possessing perfect knowledge (*kevalajñānin*); and the reality of things consists of origination, destruction, and persistence. For instance, every object such as the earth, mountains, or trees is neither produced nor destroyed in its substantial essence (*dravyātman*), because a clear continuity (*anvaya*) is observed. One should not argue that this is an inconclusive argument (*vyabhicāra*) because continuity is seen in cases like nails that have been cut and grown back again; for the continuity in such cases is not clearly established, being contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, the continuity under discussion here is not contradicted by valid knowledge, since it is established by true recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

In all individual manifestations, there is a constant difference from moment to moment, yet there is no absolute distinction; for it is stated that "even while accumulation and depletion are real, the determination of form and genus remains. Therefore, every entity exists as a substance (*dravya*), yet every entity arises and perishes through its mode (*paryāya*), because the experience of unimpeded modes is ever-present.

Nor is there any deviation [from the rule] in the case of a white conch being experienced through successive states such as yellow and so forth, because that experience is of a faltering nature; for it is certainly not of a non-faltering nature such that the destruction of the preceding form would be invariably concomitant with the production of a succeeding form while not relinquishing its function. Furthermore, the experience of a succession of states such as joy, resentment, and indifference in a substance like the living soul (*jīva*) is not of a faltering nature, because there is an absence of any subverting factor.

Now, do origination and the others differ from one another or not? If they differ, how can a single entity possess a threefold nature? If they do not differ, even so, how can a single entity possess a threefold nature? Thus, if origination and the others are distinct, how can one thing be threefold? Or, if origination and the others are non-distinct, how can one thing be threefold? If this is asked:

That is incorrect—because their difference is accepted in some respect (*kathañcit*) due to their having characteristics that are in some respect different (*kathañcid-bhinnalakṣaṇatva*). To explain: origination, destruction, and persistence are in some respect distinct, because they have distinct characteristics, like color and so forth. Nor is it unestablished that they have distinct characteristics; for indeed, the acquisition of self-nature by the non-existent, the non-separation from existence by the existent, and the persistence in the form of substance (*dravya*) are the mutually unmixed characteristics of origination and the others, which are witnessed by all the world. And these are not [entirely] distinct characteristics.

Furthermore, they cannot be mutually independent, for that would result in their non-existence, like a flower in the sky. For instance, arising alone does not exist because it is devoid of persistence and cessation, just like a tortoise’s hair; likewise, destruction alone does not exist because it is devoid of arising, for the same reason; and persistence alone does not exist because it is empty of both destruction and arising, for the same reason. Thus, one must understand that arising and the other phases exist in a real entity only as they are mutually dependent. As it has been said:
"One who seeks a jar, a crown, or gold undergoes grief, joy, or indifference—each with its respective cause—when there is destruction, arising, or persistence."

"One who is under a vow of milk does not eat curd; one who is under a vow of curd does not eat milk; one who is under a vow of non-dairy products eats neither. Therefore, an entity consists of three aspects. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is as follows: that which does not possess the nature of origination, destruction, and persistence is not a real entity at all, just like a donkey's horn; and as this is so, so is that. For this very reason, it is stated that a real entity, characterized by infinite attributes (*anantadharmaka*), is the object of valid cognition (*māna*). A real entity is "characterized by infinite attributes" because it is that in which infinite attributes—namely, modes (*paryāyas*) characterized by both generality and particularity—reside. This is precisely to demonstrate that only that which possesses the nature of origination, destruction, and persistence can logically be established as having multiple attributes.

The meaning of the verse is that there is a further employment of the term "possessing infinite attributes" (anantadharmaka), and one should not suspect tautology with the term "possessing infinite attributes" mentioned in the subsequent verse. || 57 ||
Thus has this summary of the Jaina philosophy been told, in which there is no contradiction whatsoever between what precedes and what follows. (58)

Since this treatise has as its fruit the awakening of the intellect of beginners, the author concludes by saying: "Jainadarśana... Thus, in the manner previously described, this summary of the Jaina system (*jainadarśanasaṃkṣepa*), which is directly perceptible, has been told; for a detailed exposition is beyond the scope of speech due to its unfathomable depth, this summary, the essence of its utility (*upayogasāra*), has been presented. Of what nature is it? It is "flawless" (*anagha*), meaning free from defects, because since everything that can be said is rooted in the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*), there is no room for the turbidity of error.

But [the word "tu"] has the sense of conjunction; furthermore, in that [system], there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows anywhere. Wherein—in whatever philosophical system—there is no contradiction or inconsistency of meaning at the beginning (the former) or at the end (the latter), even in the concluding portions of the texts, let alone in the twelvefold scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga*) consisting of the Buddha’s own words; for even in the traditional treatises (*pāramparya-grantha*), there is an absence of the foul odor of contradictory meanings because their subject matter is well-connected.

This is the point: we do not perceive logical consistency even in the fundamental scriptures of those other sectarians, much less in the compositions of later deceptive authors; and as for those few words concerning compassion and meritorious deeds that we occasionally hear, they too are like jewels emerged from the churning of the ocean of the nectar of your well-spoken verses, which these people grasp and, like lords of jewels, vainly pride themselves upon.
As the venerable Śrī Siddhasena Divākara said:
Whatever wealth of eloquent sayings flashes forth within our well-ascertained systems of dependent reasoning,
these are likewise mere droplets from the words of the Jina— the standard of authority for the world— which have arisen from the full great ocean.
Thus is the ultimate truth. || 58 ||

Regarding the category of deities, there is no difference between the Vaiśeṣikas and the Naiyāyikas; however, that difference exists within their respective categories (tattvas), which is now being pointed out. (59)

Although they are equal in having Śiva as their deity, because they are distinguished by specific principles (tattvas) and so forth, they are called Vaiśeṣikas; for these Vaiśeṣikas, such as the followers of Kaṇāda, there is no difference or distinction from the Naiyāyikas, the followers of Akṣapāda, regarding the deity—that is, in the acceptance of Śiva as the deity. However, there is a difference regarding the principles (tattvas), which are the secrets of the teaching; the word "tu" (but/however) is to be supplied [in the verse]. This distinction—their state of being separate from the Naiyāyikas—is pointed out, meaning it is made manifest. || 59 ||
[The view of Kaṇāda:
Substance, quality, action, and the fourth, generality;
as well as particularity and inherence—these are indeed the six categories in his system. (60)

He states those very principles with the words beginning "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth. In that system—that is, in the Vaiśeṣika system—it is certainly to be understood that there are six principles; this is the connection [of the sentence]. To the question "How? he says: "Substance, quality," and so on. The first principle is named substance (*dravya*); although there is a multiplicity of divisions, it is one due to its commonality. The second principle is named quality (*guṇa*); the word "likewise" (*tathā*) indicates other subdivisions. The third principle is designated as action (*karman*). The fourth principle is generality (*sāmānya*); the suffix *-ka* in *caturthaka* is used in its own sense (i.e., as a synonym for "fourth"). The particle *ca* denotes conjunction, and [the word] "moreover" (*anyacca*) [indicates further categories].

Regarding the view that "particularity and inherence" (*viśeṣasamavāyau*) is a copulative compound (*dvandva*)—meaning particularity (*viśeṣa*) and inherence (*samavāya*)—in that system, six principles (*tattva*) are to be known. || 60 ||
In that regard, substance is of nine kinds: earth, water, fire, air, and ether; as well as time, space, self, and mind. Qualities, moreover, are of twenty-four kinds. (61)
Touch, taste, form, smell, sound, number, disjunction, conjunction, dimension, separateness, as well as priority and posteriority; || 62 ||
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, merit and demerit, effort, mental impression, aversion, viscidity, gravity, fluidity, and velocity—these are the qualities. 63.
Throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion—this action is fivefold; however, there are two types of generality: the higher and the lower.
He states the general and specific divisions of action with the words beginning "utkṣepa" (upward throwing) and so forth.

All five varieties of action are indeed clear; by the inclusion of "going," whirling, ejecting, flowing, and so on, are subsumed. Furthermore, there are two types of generality (*sāmānya*). Which are they? He says: "the higher and the lower" (*parāpare*). "Higher and lower" means both the higher generality and the lower generality. || 64 ||

Among these, existence (sattā) is the highest [genus], while substantiality (dravyatva) and the like are lower; furthermore, the ultimate particular (viśeṣa) is definitively specified as residing in eternal substances. || 65 ||
He explains this manifestation and specific manifestation with the words beginning "therein, the supreme," and so forth.

Therein, between those two, the supreme is called existence (*sattā*), being, or the great universal (*mahāsāmānya*), because its scope is greater in comparison to subordinate universals such as substantiality (*dravyatva*). The subordinate universal is substantiality and the like; this is also designated as a "universal-particular" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). For instance: substantiality is a universal because it subsists in the nine substances, and it is a particular because it is excluded from qualities and actions; therefore, by means of a *karmadhāraya* compound, it is called a "universal-particular."

Thus, in relation to substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and the like are lower universals (*apara-sāmānya*); in relation to those, "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and the like are still lower.

Likewise, among the twenty-four qualities (*guṇa*), "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) is a universal because it resides in them, and it is a particular (*viśeṣa*) because it distinguishes them from substances and actions. Similarly, in relation to quality-ness, "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and the like are universals, and in relation to those, "blue-ness" (*nīlatva*) and the like are particulars. Likewise, among the five types of action, "action-ness" (*karmatva*) is a universal because it exists in them, and it is a particular because it distinguishes them from substances and qualities; similarly, in relation to action-ness, "upward-thrusting-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and the like should be understood.

In this regard, existence (*sattā*) is a distinct entity from substance, quality, and action. If one asks by what reasoning this is so, it is said: existence is not a substance, meaning it is other than substance, because it resides in a single substance—that is, because it subsists in each individual substance.

Like substantiality (*dravyatva*): just as substantiality, while residing individually in each of the nine substances, is not itself a substance but rather a generality (*sāmānya*) characterized as a particular (*viśeṣa*), so too is *sattā*. For the Vaiśeṣikas, a substance is either "without substance" (*adravya*), or it is "with many substances" (*anekadravya*). Among these, substances without substance are space, time, direction, the self, and atoms; substances with many substances are aggregates (*skandha*) such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. A substance that possesses only one substance is not a substance at all.
Since *sattā* possesses only one substance, it is not a substance because it differs from the definition of a substance.

Thus, existence (*sattā*) is not a quality (*guṇa*), because it does not reside in qualities, just as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) does not. For if existence were a quality, it would not reside in qualities, since qualities are themselves devoid of further qualities; yet it does reside in qualities, as in the cognition "the quality exists. Furthermore, if existence were a quality, it would not reside in actions (*karman*), since actions are devoid of action; yet the entity [existence] does reside in actions, as evidenced by the cognition "the action is existent. Therefore, existence is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*).

Now, he states the category of *viśeṣa* (particularity) with the second half-verse—beginning with "But the particular" (*viśeṣastu*). It should be understood that it is taught by the Teacher as something distinct, residing in eternal substances, according to definitive certainty.

He asks, "How so? and replies: "The ultimate particular (*antya-viśeṣa*) resides in eternal substances; for instance, the ultimate particulars residing in eternal substances are the causes of absolute differentiation. Because they are distinct from substance and the other categories, they are a separate category of reality (*padārthāntara*). Thus says Praśastakāra: 'They are called ultimate (*antya*) because they exist in the ultimates (*anteṣu*); they are called particulars (*viśeṣa*) because they differentiate their own substrates. They reside one by one in each of the eternal substances—atoms, ether, time, space, self, and mind—which are devoid of destruction or origination.'"

They are the causes of the cognition of absolute exclusion; for, in the case of cows and the like, as perceived by people such as ourselves, it is impossible for there to be causes based on differences in shape, action, parts, increase or decrease, or specific conjunctions [with universals], from which causes there arises—on each respective substrate—the exclusion of cognitions in the form "this is distinct" and "that is distinct," as well as the recognition "this is that very same one" even when the atom is removed in space and time. These are the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*); and these are indeed particulars alone, and not...

The meaning is that it possesses the nature of both a universal and a particular, like substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, because it is precisely the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) that serves as the cause [of cognition]. || 65 ||

That relation which is declared here to be the cause of the cognition "it is here" regarding entities that are inseparably established in the nature of container and contained is inherence (samavāya). || 66 ||

He states the definition of the category of inherence (*samavāya*) with the words "that which here," and so forth. In this present system, inherence is that relation which is the cause of the cognition "here" among things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relationship of substratum and superstratum—such as, for example, "the cloth is here in these threads. Inherence is the uncommon cause of such a cognition; by virtue of it, the superstratum, such as a cloth, being produced through the capacity of its own causes, becomes connected to its substratum, such as the threads, just as the action of cutting is connected to the object to be cut. This refers to "those things that are inseparably established."

The relationship of substratum and superstratum belongs to those things that have distinct bases by way of mutual exclusion; however, the mutual dissimilarity [of these categories] is to be inferred from their distinct definitions, as it is not elaborated here because this treatise is restricted solely to the description of the essential nature of the six categories. || 66 ||
And their means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are of two kinds: perception and inference.
Thus has the summary of the Vaiśeṣika doctrine been proclaimed. || 67 ||

He states the specific forms of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the words "And the means of valid cognition," and so forth. Although in the teaching of the followers of Ulūka (the Vaiśeṣikas) there are three means of valid cognition as stated by the teacher Akṣapāda, nevertheless, according to the view of Śrīdhara, only two are mentioned here. For these Vaiśeṣikas, the means of valid cognition is twofold, of two kinds. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "moreover. He asks how this is so and says: one means of valid cognition is perception (*pratyakṣa*); likewise—the word "likewise" (*tathā*) referring to the second division—is inferential (*laiṅgika*), which is inference (*anumāna*). Concluding, he says: "Thus."

The word "thus" (*evam*) indicates the manner [of exposition]. Although much more could be said with respect to the subject, the result, and so forth, nevertheless, in this manner, the summary of the Vaiśeṣika doctrine has been stated and proclaimed. || 67 ||
[The view of Jaimini]:

The followers of Jaimini, however, assert that there exists no deity whatsoever characterized by such attributes as omniscience and the like, whose word could serve as a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). (68)

He states the sixth view, beginning with "The followers of Jaimini, however," and so forth. Those who belong to the sage Jaimini are the *Jaiminīyas*; here, the secondary suffix *iyap* is used in the sense of "descendants" (such as sons and grandsons). Among them, some are proponents of the *Uttara-mīmāṃsā* (the later inquiry) and others are proponents of the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā* (the earlier inquiry). Of these, the proponents of the *Uttara-mīmāṃsā* are the Vedāntins; for they are devoted to establishing the doctrine of the absolute non-duality (*advaita*) of Brahman alone. Wielding logical arguments to refute the [dualistic] meanings of words, they establish themselves upon the principle of the "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*). As they say: "If the cause contains existence within itself, then it is non-existent."
If the cause does not contain existence within itself, then it is therefore non-existent.
The more these things are investigated, the more they fall apart;
if this [emptiness] itself is pleasing to you regarding these objects, then who are we [to object]?
Taking up the single Brahma-weapon and never accounting for any other,
there is no defeat for that firm hero in the playful contests of battle.
Thus, when the proponent and the opponent dance about, relying on the consensus of all the world and its scriptures,
what could be the status of the corresponding cognition of objects and linguistic usage?
For those two [theories] which are subject to suspicion through various philosophical systems,
the only possible recourse is to resort to the feet of the doctrine of ineffability (anirvaktavyatāvāda).

Where do these arguments establishing the non-duality of the Supreme Brahman—which resemble the rows of waves in the final mass of waters agitated by the winds at the time of universal dissolution—culminate as they surge forth, producing delight for the wise? Since those logical reasonings were not set down by the author of the Sūtras and for fear of excessive prolixity, they are not elaborated here; however, they should be understood from the *Khaṇḍana* and the *Mahātarka* by those who are diligent.

Furthermore, the proponents of Pūrvamīmāṃsā are twofold—the Prābhākaras and the Bhāṭṭas—who respectively propound five and six means of valid cognition; however, here the author of the Sūtras has generally designated only the Jaiminīyas as proponents of Pūrvamīmāṃsā.

Furthermore, those followers of Jaimini say: they declare that there exists no deity whatsoever characterized by attributes such as omniscience, whose word—his speech—could constitute valid knowledge (*māna*). There is no deity distinguished by qualities such as being omniscient or having a diverse nature, whose word might attain the status of authority; for, since there is no distinction from the human body, [any such being] would be prone to deception like a wicked man. The meaning is that there is an absence of any person distinguished by qualities such as omniscience.

If it is argued that there exists a certain particular person who is omniscient, because otherwise the sovereignty indicated by the umbrella, chowries, and so forth—which signify the empire over the three worlds—would be inexplicable, given that he is served by gods and asuras acting as his servants; we say no. This has already been refuted by the presentation of the elaborate arguments you yourself have stated, as follows:
"The splendors such as the arrival of gods, celestial chariots, and chowries are seen even among magicians; therefore, you are not great in our eyes."

Now, one might think: "Just as even beginningless impurity in gold attains purity when being cleansed through processes such as alkaline treatment, clay, and heating in a crucible (*puṭapāka*), why should it not be possible for the Self as well, since its impurities are removed by the continuous practice of knowledge and so forth? That too is not the case—for when there is merely a similarity in the practice, the resulting purity remains in that very same state [of potentiality]. As it has been said: "Even though the possibility of the practice of leaping exists equally for both Garuḍa and the monkey, there is no equality in their actual leaping."
Moreover, even one who possesses great power of movement is not capable of climbing to the peak of a mountain that is not low, if he is lame.
And it has been said:
"He who, though unable to leap even ten cubits into the air, [cannot reach the summit]."
One is not able to travel a hundred yojanas, even with hundreds of practices.

Now, let it be that a human being does not possess omniscience; let it belong to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and the like, for they are gods, and in them an excellence surpassing [that of others] is possible. As Kumārila said: "Even so, because they are the causes of the Vedas, let Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara be omniscient at will; but what is the use of omniscience for a human being?"

Even this [knowledge] cannot be conceived as possible for those who are consumed by the suppression of passion and hatred and the favoring of attachment, since perception does not establish it—according to the statement that "the eye and other senses grasp what is connected and present. Nor is there inference, because inference operates only upon an object already perceived through perception. Nor is there scripture, because an omniscient being is unestablished and thus remains a subject of dispute.

Nor is there an analogy, precisely because such a thing does not exist; nor is there presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), since no logical mark (*liṅga*) is observed that is otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapanna*) as proving an omniscient being. At most, it remains established that the omniscient being is within the scope of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*). And the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: "An omniscient being does not exist, because he transcends the scope of perception and the other [means of knowledge], like the horn of a hare. || 68 ||
Therefore, since there is no direct perceiver of supersensuous objects, the determination of their truthfulness must come from the eternal sentences of the Veda. (69)

Now, how is there a determination of reality as it truly exists? To this he says: "Therefore, of supersensuous objects... Because of the absence of authoritative persons—due to the lack of any person who is a direct seer or knower of supersensuous objects (atīndriyārtha), that is, things beyond the range of the eyes—and because of the eternal and perpetual Vedic statements which are non-human utterances, there occurs "the determination of the reality of things as they are," that is, the discernment of the true nature of the properties and so forth of objects as they exist; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Furthermore, the non-human authorship of the Vedas is as follows:
For he is without hands or feet, yet he grasps; he sees without eyes, and he hears without ears.
He knows the universe, yet there is no knower of him; him they call the foremost, the Great Person.

"By means of such meditations as 'the white ones are [like] water' (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19) and so forth, one should cultivate [this state] preceded by the setting aside of defects such as passion and hatred. || 69 ||
Therefore, first of all, the recitation of the Vedas should be performed with diligence;
thereafter, the inquiry into dharma, which is the means for accomplishing dharma, must be undertaken.
Now, he states the instruction on reality (*tattvopadeśa*) which establishes the object as it truly exists, beginning with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).

Since the determination of reality arises precisely from the performance of what is enjoined in the Vedas, for that very reason, one must first of all diligently apply effort to the study of the Vedas—the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāma*, and *Atharva* Vedas. Their "study" means their establishment upon the surface of the throat through constant recitation; mere hearing does not ensure a firm and correct understanding. Thereafter, one must undertake—that is, perform—the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) Dharma, which is the cause for accumulating merit to be accomplished and which consists of the nature of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted as taught in the Vedas.
The meaning is that one must strive toward the injunctions of the subjects declared in the Vedas. || 70 ||
Dharma is characterized by instigation; instigation, however, is speech that prompts action toward an activity, as in the example:
"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with fire. (71)

He explains precisely the instruction on the dharma taught in the Vedas with the words beginning "characterized by injunction" (*nodanālakṣaṇa*). That dharma which has injunction alone as its defining characteristic is "characterized by injunction. The author of the Sūtras states its very nature: "But [they] say that injunction is an impelling statement" (*tu punarnodanāṃ kriyāṃ pravarttakaṃ vacaḥ prāhuḥ*). The meaning is that they call "injunction" (*nodanā*) the statement that impels action within the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*) which establishes heaven and other such goals. Out of compassion for his students, he provides an illustration by means of that very Sūtra: "Just as one desiring heaven should sacrifice to Agni" (*svaḥkāmo 'gniṃ yajed yathā*).

In whatever manner—that is, by whichever method—a person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*), one who longs for the celestial realm, should sacrifice to Agni, that is, should perform the fire-rite; as it is said in that Sūtra: "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra. || 71 ||
Perception, inference, and verbal testimony, together with comparison, presumptive testimony, and non-existence—these are the six means of valid cognition according to Jaimini. (72)
He states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the words "perception, inference," and so forth.

The connection is that for Jaimini—the proponent of the earlier Vedānta—six means of valid cognition are to be known; although in the view of the Prābhākaras there are five means of valid cognition and only for the Bhāṭṭas are there six, nevertheless, here the author of the text mentions the number six in general. The names of the means of valid cognition are established by the very recitation [of the words]. (72)
Among these, perception is the cognition that arises when there is contact of the sense organs with their objects;
inference, moreover, is the arising of an understanding in the self through a mark (liṅga). (73)

He states the etymological explanation with the words beginning "tatra" (therein). "Therein" means within that group of six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). When there is a "contact" (*samprayoga*)—that is, a conjunction—of the "senses" (*akṣāṇām*), i.e., the organs, with their objects; when there is "cognition" (*mati*), i.e., the intellect (*buddhi*), the awareness that "this is [it]" belonging to those who are "existent," meaning those whose senses are unimpaired—that is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); the word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. Although the pronouns "yat" and "tat" are not explicitly stated, they are to be understood as connected to the sense. Regarding the word "existent" (*satām*): it refers to the wise ones whose sense-objects are not defective. By this much, it is shown that even the delusion of water in a mirage and the delusion of silver in mother-of-pearl, though produced by the contact of sense and object, are excluded.

Because the perceiver lacks unimpaired sense faculties, that [perception of the self] does not enter the category of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). He states [the means of] inference (*anumāna*): "Furthermore, inference is the arising of cognition in the self; it is inferential (*laiṅgika*). The meaning is that whatever the self infers by itself, that is inference. Although there is no difference in the verbal expression for both *anumāna* and *laiṅgika*, the distinction between them should be understood from their etymologies: it is called *anumāna* because it is inferred (*anumīyate*), and *laiṅgika* because it is born from a mark (*liṅga*). The mention of both terms, however, is solely for the sake of instructing the ignorant. || 73 ||
Verbal [simile] is proclaimed as that which arises from the distinction between the eternal [word] and [the object];
it is the means for making known an unfamiliar thing through its similarity to a familiar object. (74)

Verbal testimony (*śābda*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arising from the eternal Veda; that is to say, it is the means of valid cognition born from the eternal and permanent Veda. The eternality of the Vedas is due precisely to their being authorless (*apauruṣeya*). He now states the definition of analogy (*upamāna*): that which is the establishment of an unknown object through its similarity to a known object—that is, a thing whose referent is already understood—is proclaimed as the means of valid cognition called analogy.

For example, a forest-dweller who knows the true nature of a cow but not the true nature of a gavaya says to a city-dweller: "As is a cow, so is a gavaya. "O sir! You know that an object possessing hooves, a hump, a tail, a dewlap, and so forth, is a cow; a gavaya should be understood to have that same nature. This is analogy (*upamāna*). Although these two pronouns (*yat* and *tat*) are not explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra, they must be supplied for the sake of establishing the relationship between the meanings. 74.

When, due to the impossibility of a perceived fact, the postulation of some other fact is made by the force of which that [perceived fact] is accounted for, this is cited as presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). || 75 ||

He states *arthāpatti* (presumption) with the words "by the non-occurrence of a perceived object," and so forth. This *arthāpatti* is "cited" or mentioned; that is to say, the means of valid cognition known as *arthāpatti* is proclaimed. That by the force of which the postulation (*kalpanā*)—the mental construction (*saṅghaṭanā*)—of some unperceived object is performed: by what non-occurrence of a perceived object? By the non-occurrence, the impossibility, or the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of a perceived, familiar object characterized by perception, such as Devadatta’s corpulence and the like. For example: "The corpulent Devadatta does not eat during the day"; [this is established] by the otherwise-unaccountability of his corpulence.

Regarding the meaning "he necessarily eats at night": since corpulence is difficult to account for without eating, and he does not eat during the day, this necessitates the knowledge that he eats unseen at night; thus, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). || 75 ||

Where the five means of valid cognition do not arise with respect to the nature of an object, there the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāva) functions for the purpose of apprehending the existence of that object. (76)

He states the means of valid cognition for non-existence (*abhāva*) with the words beginning "the fivefold means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇapañcakam*). The connection is as follows: where, in a category of object such as non-existence, the aforementioned fivefold means of valid cognition do not arise, there the status of non-existence as a means of valid cognition is to be known. To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "for the sake of understanding the existence of an entity. This means: the existence of an entity that is of the nature of non-existence, such as a bare ground; its existence consists in the presence of the absence of a jar or the like; "understanding" that is its introduction into the path of valid cognition; "for the sake of that" means for the purpose of that, i.e., for that reason.

Now, how can non-existence (abhāva) possess the status of a means of valid cognition (prāmāṇya)? First of all, perception (pratyakṣa) is the determination of a real entity through the method of agreement and difference, such as "this ground is indeed not a jar" and so forth; it thus excludes any object beyond that which is of the nature of mere non-existence. Based on what object, then, could there be the validity of non-existence? If you say it is based on the absence of a jar on a bare ground, do not say so—because the apprehension of the ground as being restricted by the absence of a jar is unestablished. As it has been said: "First of all, the cognition 'it does not exist' does not arise through the sense organ."
For conjunction occurs only with the objective aspect of an entity, due to the suitability of the sense organ.
Having apprehended the positive existence of an object and having remembered its counter-correlate,
a mental cognition of non-existence arises independently of the sense organs.

Thus, at the time of apprehending the knowledge of non-existence (*nāstitājñāna*), it is indeed the non-existence itself that possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*). It is merely because the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) arises from sensory contact that it wanders within the domain of the five means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); yet, it initiates worldly activity well-known even to women, children, and cowherds. However, the negative aspect (*abhāvāṃśa*), because it lies outside the scope of the five means of knowledge and because it is useful for the apprehension of the bare ground alone, receives the designation of "non-existence as a means of knowledge" (*abhāvapramāṇa*). Thus, it is established that the validity of non-existence is also logically consistent. || 76 ||
This summary of the Jaiminīya doctrine has also been presented;
thus, the brief exposition of the tenets of the orthodox schools has been completed. (77)
Concluding, he says: "Of the Jaiminīya doctrine as well.

By the word "as well" (api), it is indicated that this summary has been presented—not only for other philosophical systems, but also for the Jaiminīya doctrine. Because there is a great deal to be said, it is impossible to state everything in its entirety within a mere commentary; therefore, only a summary has been proclaimed.

Now, having stated the summary as accepted by the authors of the Sūtras, he provides the conclusion with the word "evam" (thus). "Evam" means in this manner; thus has the brief account been given here of the proponents of theism—those who maintain belief in the next world, merit, and demerit—namely the Buddhists, Naiyāyikas, Sāṅkhyas, Jains, Vaiśeṣikas, and followers of Jaimini. The meaning is that what was to be said has been stated in summary. || 77 ||
Those other than the Naiyāyikas do not consider there to be a distinction [between them] and the Vaiśeṣikas; in their view, there are only five proponents of the doctrine of existence (astikavādins).
He states another distinction with the words "from the Naiyāyika school," and so forth.

Other teachers do not consider there to be a difference between the Naiyāyika school and the Vaiśeṣikas, because they hold that there is a single presiding deity for both systems; thus, they do not accept them as separate philosophical systems (darśana). From their perspective, those who maintain the doctrine of the existence of the soul (āstikavādins) are only five.
It is said that in his view, the number of the six systems of philosophy is completed by the inclusion of the Lokāyata doctrine; therefore, he explains that system of thought. (79)
He explains how the well-known number of six systems of philosophy (*darśana*) in the world is fulfilled: with the words beginning "ṣaḍdarśana" and so forth.

For those who, considering the Naiyāyika and Vaiśeṣika to be of a single nature, maintain that there are only five systems of philosophy, in their view the number of six systems is completed by including the Lokāyata doctrine. The word "tu" (but/then) indicates a distinction; "kila" refers to the tradition of the most authoritative teachers. By that reason, that system—the Cārvāka doctrine—is being described, and its essential nature is stated. || 79 ||
[The Cārvāka doctrine:
The Lokāyatas say thus: "There is no god, nor is there liberation;
neither merit nor demerit exist, nor is there any fruit of virtuous or sinful deeds. (80)

He states that very point with the words beginning "the Lokāyatas": the Lokāyatas are nihilists; they speak in this manner. How so? He says: there is no omniscient being and so forth; there is no *nirvṛti*, which is liberation; and furthermore, two other things do not exist—what are they? *Dharma* and *adharma*; this is a copulative compound (*dvandva*), meaning merit and demerit do not exist. There is no fruit in the form of heaven, hell, and so on, resulting from merit and demerit, *dharma* and *adharma*; for if merit and demerit are absent, from where could that fruit arise? And so forth.

Showing that very same [view] as it is stated in their own scripture, he says with derision: "And thus is their doctrine. Here, "and thus" (*tathā ca*) is used for demonstration; "their doctrine" (*tanmatam*) refers, by the context, to the doctrine of the nihilists (*nāstika*). || 80 ||
"This world is only as much as is within the range of the senses, O blessed lady! Behold the 'track of the wolf' (vṛkapada), as it is called by those of great learning. (81)
He asks "How so? and replies with the words "This much alone," and so forth.

This world—that is, *saṃsāra*—is only this much, precisely this much: as much as is the range of the senses. The sense organ is fivefold, distinguished as touch, taste, smell, sight, and hearing; its range is its object. There exists only that reality which is manifested by the five senses, and nothing else. Here, by the use of the term "world" (*loka*), there is an inclusion of the entire multitude of objects situated within the world.

Likewise, others claim that heaven, hell, and so forth are to be attained through merit and demerit; that is invalid precisely because they are not perceived. If you argue that something exists even though it is imperceptible, then let there also be the existence of a rabbit’s horn, the son of a barren woman, and the like. For instance: by the sense of touch, states such as softness, hardness, cold, heat, oiliness, and roughness are apprehended;
by the sense of taste, pungent, astringent, sour, sweet, and bitter flavors, as well as things to be licked, sucked, and drunk, are experienced.
By the sense of smell, the successive emanations of fragrance from fragrant substances such as musk, sandalwood, camphor, and agallochum are discerned;
by the sense of sight, the multitude of moving and stationary objects—such as mountains, cities, walls, jars, cloths, pillars, lotuses, humans, cattle, and wild beasts—is perceived;
and by the sense of hearing, the sweet sounds of the swaying and playful modulations of rhythm, measure, and melody being proclaimed by renowned singers and travelers are heard.

Thus, only the reality of things as directly perceived through these five modes of perception enters the domain of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); all other means of knowledge are rejected precisely because they lack any corresponding experience, like a flower in the sky.

And those whose mental dispositions are obsessed by a thirst for the pleasures of heaven, liberation, and so forth—desiring even that which has never been touched, tasted, smelled, seen, or heard—and who waste their lives through the grinding toil of performing most difficult austerities and the like, commit a great act of rashness.

Furthermore—if the world were accepted as existing even through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it could not be denied at all. For a poor man might easily dispel his misery simply by contemplating, "I possess a heap of gold"; and even a slave, by assuming lordship within his own mind, might cast off his servitude. Thus, no one would ever experience the impurity of their own undesirable condition. In this way, there would be no relationship of master and servant, nor any distinction between the poor and the wealthy, and consequently, the entire order of the world would collapse. Therefore, it is well established that only that which falls within the range of the senses is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

And for those talkative ones who do not cease, asserting the validity of inference, scripture, and so forth, and establishing the pleasure and pain of heaven, hell, and the like as attainable through meritorious and sinful activities—he provides an illustration for them:

"O blessed lady, look at the wolf's footprint! Just as a certain man, having fashioned a wolf's footprint by placing his own fingers upon a patch of dust leveled by a very gentle breeze, says to his beloved who is filled with curiosity at the sight of the wolf's track—"O blessed lady, look at the wolf's footprint"—what is the meaning? It is that the clever lover, by means of the mere placement of his fingers, entices his innocent beloved, who does not know the ultimate truth, to satisfy her insistence on seeing the wolf's footprints.

Just as [the previous examples] have filled [the world with falsehood], so too these rogues disguised as Dharma, intent on deceiving others, display some semblance of strength through inference, scripture, and the like, and thus pointlessly cast deluded people into the perilous thicket of what is fit or unfit to eat, who may or may not be approached, and what is to be abandoned or adopted—enticing them with the vast enjoyment of pleasures obtainable upon reaching heaven—and they produce a blindness toward true piety in the gullible. And while elevating this very same matter to the status of authoritative proof, they say that which those of great learning who know the ultimate truth declare;
such is the meaning of the verse to be cited hereafter. || 81 ||
Drink and eat, O lady of noble beauty! That which has passed, O fair-limbed one, belongs no more to you.
For what has gone does not return, O timid one; this body is merely a collection of elements. 82.

He states what ought to be done with the words beginning "Drink," etc.: "O you of born beauty!"—since these designations emphasize the state [of being], this is an address to her who possesses "born beauty," namely, the possession of a face, eyes, and so forth. "Drink"—perform the drinking of wine and the like, without regard for the confusion of distinctions between what is drinkable and undrinkable. Not only drink, but "eat" as well; consume meat and such, without consideration for what is edible and inedible. Alternatively, "drink" means perform the drinking of lips and so forth, and "eat" means enjoy sensual pleasures; this is an instruction for one who desires, meaning: "Make your own youth fruitful."

Now, suspecting the opponent's argument that "beauty is indeed easily regained even in another life through the power of merit," he says: "O fair-limbed one! That which has passed—that youth and so forth which has already gone by—is not yours again; rather, the meaning is that you will only become worn out by old age. Regarding the address "O born-beautiful one" (*jāta-śobhane*) and "O fair-limbed one" (*vara-gātri*): although these two addresses have the same meaning, there is no fault of tautology because of the excess of respect and affection. As it is said: "There is no repetition in cases of restatement, respect, emphasis, intense meaning, application, cause, envy, slight, agitation, wonder, counting, and recollection."

One might object: "If one eats and drinks according to one's own desire without restraint, there will be an insurmountable succession of hardships in the next world; whereas in the accumulation of merit, youth and such things become easily available even in another birth. Refuting this further objection, he says: "For what has passed does not return, O timid one! O timid one—O you who are agitated by the fear of suffering to be experienced in hell and other realms merely because of the words of others! That which has passed, such as the pleasures and youth of this life, does not return; it does not arrive in the next world. Therefore, the neglect of worldly pleasures for the sake of performing arduous deeds such as asceticism out of a longing for happiness in the next world is futile. This is the meaning.

Now, if it is argued that because of the existence of a relationship between the produced and the producer, pleasure, pain, and so forth must necessarily be experienced with a cause even in the next world by means of this body—[the author] replies: "This body is a mere collection. This body, the physical frame, is a mere collection (*samudaya*); *samudaya* means a gathering or a conglomeration. It is merely the conjunction of the four elements to be described hereafter. The word "mere" (*mātra*) is used for emphasis; the body is simply a connection with the four elements, and nothing more.

The meaning is that [the self] is dependent upon the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, which are the results of the ripening of virtuous and non-virtuous actions from previous existences. Furthermore, these conjunctions [with the body] are momentary and perishable, like a flock of birds perched on the branches of a tree; therefore, without regard for the next world, drink and eat as you please—this is the meaning of the verse. || 82 ||
Furthermore, earth, water, fire, and air constitute the four elements; consciousness is their ground, for their measure is indeed derived from the senses alone. (83)

He states [their view on] consciousness with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*). The word "furthermore" (*kiñca*) is used for the purpose of illustration: earth (*pṛthvī*), water (*jala*), fire (*tejas*), and air (*vāyu*)—this is the quartet of elements (*bhūtacatuṣṭaya*). For those Cārvākas, this is the "ground of consciousness" (*caitanyabhūmi*), meaning the cause of the production of consciousness. The meaning is that all four elements, having come together, produce consciousness as a single integrated whole (*sapiṇḍa*). Furthermore, "measure" (*māna*)—that is, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is certainly only that which is born of the senses; the meaning is that perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone is the single means of valid cognition. || 83 ||

Just as the power of intoxication arises from the components of wine, so too does the body and its like arise from the aggregation of the elements, such as earth and the rest; in that same way, the state of being a self exists [as a mere designation].

One might ask: "How can the arising of consciousness in a body produced by the conjunction of the four elements be understood? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the aggregation of the elements such as earth," and so forth. This means when there is a combination or union (*saṃhati*)—that is, a meeting (*melana*)—of those elements which are earth, water, fire, and air; "likewise" (*tathā*) indicates that the emergence of the body and so on occurs. By the word "and so on" (*ādi*), other objects such as mountains and the like should also be understood as being born solely from the conjunction of these four. He states an illustration: "just as," and so forth.

Just as the power of intoxication—the state of being maddening—arises from the ingredients of liquor such as molasses and dhātakī flowers, so too, through its connection with the four elements, consciousness arises in the body; that is to say, it becomes sentient once it has been produced. || 84 ||
Therefore, the Cārvākas maintained that the world’s delusion consists in abandoning what is perceived and engaging with what is unperceived. 85.
This being the case, he states the conclusion preceded by that instruction with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The word "therefore" serves as a reminder of what was previously stated. Because of that aforementioned cause—namely, the abandonment of the seen (*dṛṣṭa-parityāga*), which is the happiness corresponding to drinkable and undrinkable, edible and inedible, approachable and unapproachable objects, experienced through direct perception—the engagement (*pravṛtti*) consists in turning toward the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), such as the happiness of the next world achievable through arduous practices like asceticism. The particle *ca* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*).

Because of the necessary connection between "that" (yat) and "this" (tat), it should be understood that the relationship [of the following] pertains to the half-verse. The Cārvākas, also known as the Lokāyatikas, have asserted—that is, they have accepted—that this is the delusion and ignorance of the world. For people who are deluded, whose knowledge is illuminated by the presentation of the words of deceivers, abandon worldly happiness for the sake of a thirst for heaven and liberation; thus, having abandoned the happiness available here, they pointlessly disregard the happiness already in their hands through asceticism, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and so forth, out of a thirst for heaven and liberation. || 85 ||
The joy that arises among people from the occurrence or non-occurrence of what is to be accomplished is considered by them to be useless; yet it is not at all beyond the reach of space. (86)

The recurrence or attainment of some desired object, and the cessation or absence of some undesired object—the joy that arises or is produced in people in the world because of these two—is considered by those Ājīvikas to be purposeless, devoid of intention, and empty; the meaning is that pleasure, pain, and so forth, which are achieved through merit and demerit earned in worldly existence, do not exist at all. Furthermore, that joy is no more than space (ākāśa); for just as space is empty, so too this joy is merely of the nature of non-existence. || 86 ||
Thus has this summary of the Lokāyata doctrine been set forth;
its subject matter and essential meaning should be carefully considered by those of keen intellect. (87)
Thus ends the *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya* composed by the venerable Haribhadrasūri.

He states the conclusion: "In the Lokāyata doctrine as well, it is thus. In this manner, by this method, this summary has been presented even regarding the Lokāyata doctrine; the word "api" (also) is used in a cumulative sense, meaning that the summary is stated not only in the doctrines of others, but also in the Lokāyata doctrine.

Now, having examined the *Sarvadarśanasammatasaṅgraha*, which consists of the manifold conceptual chatter and disputes imagined by one another, the author provides instruction on what ought to be done for those living beings who are bewildered as to what should be done—beginning with the words "The subject matter... (*abhidheya*). The meaning of the essential purport (*tātparyārtha*) of the subject matter must be thoroughly investigated by those of superior intellect (*subuddhi*), that is, by the learned. The "subject matter" (*abhidheya*) refers to the nature of the philosophical systems (*darśana*) which is to be explained and established as a constituent part of liberation; the "essential purport" (*tātparyārtha*) of that is its core meaning, which is to be deliberated upon. Regarding the phrase "by those of superior intellect":
this refers to those whose intellect is pure and free from partiality (*pakṣapāta*), and not to those who are gripped by dogmatic obstinacy (*kadāgraha*).
As it has been said:
"Alas, one who is dogmatic seeks to bring logic to that very point where his mind is already fixed;
for the mind of one free from partiality finds its resting place wherever it may be."

Even though the various systems of philosophy possess an identical ultimate essence, a deluded living being may develop conflicting views regarding their distinct teachings. Consequently, due to such attachment to all of them, it becomes difficult for him to achieve the means to heaven and liberation. Therefore, the true meaning must be investigated, just as it was deliberated upon by the ancients:
"The Dharma of the Sugata is to be heard; that of the Arhat is to be practiced; the Vedic [Dharma] is to be employed in worldly affairs; and the Supreme Śiva is to be meditated upon."

Having reflected on these and other such points, that which is conducive to the highest good must be accepted as a secret by those of discerning intellect; such is the meaning of the final verse. || 87 ||
The Sūtra consists of eighty-seven verses; the extent of the Commentary is determined to be one thousand two hundred and fifty-two Anuṣṭubh verses.
Thus ends the *Laghuvṛtti* composed by Maṇibhadra on the *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya* written by the venerable Haribhadrasūri.
